Leila boarded the train at dawn and placed a notebook beside the window. The route covered 840 kilometers, and she divided 840 by 70 to calculate 12 hours of travel. After the first junction, she added 126 and 84 to record 210 kilometers completed. She subtracted 210 from 840 and wrote 630 kilometers remaining. The carriage had 18 rows with 4 seats each; she multiplied 18 by 4 and entered 72 seats beneath the distance figures. Fields gave way to warehouses, then stretches of gravel beside the tracks. During a station stop, Leila counted 6 platform lamps in each of 3 groups and calculated 6 times 3 as 18. She divided her 24 crackers into 4 portions of 6 and ate one portion. By evening, the notebook contained columns of distances, seat counts, and intervals between stations. She closed it when the train reached the final platform.

Ana placed her bag beneath the window and sat beside the aisle. The train left the station, passing warehouses before reaching open fields. She took a book from her coat pocket and read several pages. When the conductor came through the carriage, she held out her ticket, then returned it to the pocket. Outside, farm buildings appeared between stretches of trees. Ana closed the book and unwrapped a sandwich over its paper covering. She ate, folded the paper, and put it in her bag. At the next station, passengers boarded with suitcases and shopping bags. The train continued past gardens, retaining walls, and rows of houses. Ana walked to the end of the carriage to fill her water bottle. Back at her place, she set the bottle on the table and opened her book again. By the time the overhead lights came on, fields had replaced the houses beyond the window.

Lukas boarded the train before sunrise and placed his bag on the rack above his seat. He took off his coat, folded it across his knees, and looked through the window as the platform moved out of view. Warehouses gave way to fields, then to rows of houses beside the tracks. After the conductor checked his ticket, Lukas opened a book and read several pages. At a station, passengers entered carrying suitcases and paper cups. He moved his feet beneath his seat to leave the aisle clear. Later, he unwrapped a sandwich and ate it over its paper wrapper. The train passed through tunnels and stopped beneath a glass station roof. Lukas walked to the carriage door, stretched his legs, and returned to his seat. By evening, the overhead lamps showed in the window alongside the passing buildings. He put his book away and kept his ticket in his coat pocket.

Leila’s train crossed the plains through its second afternoon, with three carriages behind the dining car and mountains ahead. On her lap lay a blue wool blanket she had knitted during the journey, its final corner still bristling with needles. Her phone had shown no signal for hours. She checked it at every station, then returned to the stubborn stitches. Beyond the mountain tunnel, the screen lit up. A photograph arrived first: a tiny face beneath a striped hospital cap. Then came the message that both mother and baby were doing well, and that her daughter wanted her there tonight. Leila pressed the phone against her mouth. Her shoulders bounced; a laugh escaped into the quiet carriage. She showed the photograph to the passenger opposite, then looked again herself. Ten fingers. That ridiculous little nose. Outside, the signals turned green, and the train carried her onward, right on time.

Ana boarded the train at six and placed a notebook beside the window. The route covered 960 kilometers over 12 hours, so she calculated 960 divided by 12 equaled 80 kilometers per hour. Between stations, fields passed behind rows of utility poles. She counted 24 poles in one stretch and 18 in another; 24 plus 18 equaled 42. Each carriage had 16 rows with 4 seats per row, and she wrote that 16 multiplied by 4 equaled 64 seats. After the train covered 375 kilometers, she subtracted 375 from 960 and recorded 585 kilometers remaining. At a station, several passengers exchanged places with others on the platform. Ana measured two sections of the printed route with a ruler: 7 centimeters plus 9 centimeters equaled 16 centimeters. She folded the map along its existing creases. Later, she divided 180 minutes by 60, noted 3 hours, and returned the notebook to her bag.

The overnight train carried Leila north through wheat fields, freight yards, and towns with a single light above each platform. She had packed two oranges and the cardigan her father always said was too thin. At every stop, she checked the remaining distance and rehearsed how she would walk into his hospital room without mentioning the years between visits. Near dawn, her phone vibrated. A nurse spoke for less than a minute. Leila kept the phone against her ear after the call ended, listening to the wheels beneath the carriage. Then she took out an orange and pressed her thumb into its skin until juice ran down her wrist. There would be no room to enter, no opportunity to let him interrupt her apology. Across the aisle, a passenger offered a tissue. She folded it into smaller and smaller squares while the train continued north, carrying her toward a station where nobody would be waiting.

Lukas boarded the train at six and placed his notebook beside the window. The journey covered 840 kilometers, and at an average of 70 kilometers per hour, 840 divided by 70 equaled 12 hours. He wrote the calculation beneath the date. The carriage had 18 rows with 4 seats each; 18 multiplied by 4 equaled 72 seats. After counting 29 occupied seats, he calculated that 72 minus 29 left 43 unoccupied. Outside, fields gave way to warehouses and then more fields. At the next station, 8 passengers entered and 3 departed, so 29 plus 8 minus 3 equaled 34 passengers. Lukas turned a page. He had brought 6 sandwiches, each cut into 2 pieces; 6 multiplied by 2 made 12 pieces. He ate 2, leaving 10. During the afternoon, he recorded kilometer markers at regular intervals. The train continued through several tunnels, and he closed the notebook when the carriage lights came on.

Ana boarded the train carrying a red canvas bag and a ticket printed with burgundy borders. Her seat had crimson upholstery, and a maroon curtain hung beside the wide window. For the first three hours, red brick warehouses gave way to fields divided by rust-red fences. She placed a scarlet notebook on the folding table and copied the names of stations from a red timetable. At noon, an attendant brought tomato soup in a white bowl on a vermilion tray. Ana ate, replaced the lid on her red water bottle, and turned another page. Through the afternoon, the train crossed plateaus where copper-red soil lay beneath rows of low shrubs. By evening, ruby lamps along the carriage ceiling cast red light over the aisle. She arranged her burgundy coat across her knees while the wheels continued their regular passage toward a station marked on her map with a small red square.

Leila boarded the coastal train before sunrise, carrying a canvas bag with a timetable and a chart of the adjacent sea. For the first three hours, the tracks followed beaches where small waves spread across bands of sand. Beyond the carriage window, fishing boats moved between buoys, and gulls stood along harbor walls. She ate bread at a folding table while the train rounded an inlet lined with oyster beds. By midday, the tide had exposed channels through the mudflats, with wading birds spaced along their edges. The railway crossed several river mouths on low bridges, each offering another view toward the open ocean. Leila marked the stations on her chart as cargo ships passed offshore. During the afternoon, salt gathered on the window, partly obscuring a chain of coastal villages. After fourteen hours, she left the train at a port where ferries crossed the basin beneath fixed white lights.

Leila’s train had crossed three provinces by midnight and was climbing through the mountains beneath a sky without stars. She folded her coat against the window and counted the remaining hours until morning. Beyond the glass, scattered lights disappeared as the track entered a tunnel. Then a sharp crack whipped through the carriage, followed by a grinding noise beneath her feet. Her cup slid off the table. The train gathered speed. Across the aisle, a sleeping passenger lurched forward, and the ceiling lights flickered out. Leila gripped the armrests so tightly that her nails bent. Somewhere ahead lay the viaduct she had seen on the route map, a thin line stretched over a gorge. The grinding stopped, but the rushing wheels only grew louder. She reached for the emergency handle with a shaking hand. It hung loose when she pulled it. In the darkness, she braced her feet against the seat opposite and waited for the tunnel to end.

Ana’s train crossed the plains beneath a low October sky, its windows streaked with rain. She had packed two oranges, a clean blouse, and the book her father had asked her to read aloud when she arrived. For seventeen hours, she watched stations slide past and measured the remaining distance with her thumb on a folded timetable. Beyond the mountains, her phone rang. A nurse told her that her father had died six minutes earlier. Ana kept the phone against her ear after the call ended. The carriage rocked; someone unwrapped a sandwich. She opened the book and found the scrap of paper marking their place halfway through a chapter. Her throat closed around a breath. She pressed the paper flat against her knee, then folded over it until her forehead touched the seat ahead. Outside, the tracks continued toward the room where nobody would ask her to turn another page.

Lukas sat beside the window as the overnight train crossed a plain of harvested fields. Above his seat, a small suitcase held clean shirts and the slippers his mother had requested. He had booked the earliest train after the hospital called, but repairs had kept it standing outside a junction for three hours. At dawn, his phone vibrated. He listened with one hand pressed flat against the little table. Then he asked the caller to repeat the time. The train had still been at the junction. After the call ended, he opened his suitcase and took out the slippers. He brushed a loose thread from one heel, then put them on the empty seat beside him. His throat tightened until swallowing hurt. For the remaining six hours, he watched stations slide past and kept thinking that she had asked for something so small, and he had not brought it in time.

Leila boarded the train carrying a canvas bag and a folded coat. She placed the bag beneath her seat, hung the coat on a hook, and checked the destination printed on her ticket. Beyond the window, platforms gave way to warehouses, fields, and rows of houses. She opened a book and read until the attendant came through the carriage. After showing her ticket, she took a sandwich from her bag and unfolded its paper wrapper on the tray. The train stopped at several stations during the afternoon. Passengers entered and left, placing luggage on the racks above the seats. Leila drank water, put the wrapper away, and walked along the aisle to the washroom. When she returned, the window showed farmland crossed by narrow roads. She read another chapter, then closed the book. As the carriage lights came on, she took out a container of rice and ate with a spoon.

Ana’s train crossed the mountain plateau on the second night of its journey, its windows reflecting rows of sleeping passengers. She had spent the day counting tunnels and eating bread from a paper bag. Near midnight, a metallic bang travelled beneath the carriage. Her cup slid across the table as the train began gathering speed downhill. A conductor hurried past, pulling at a radio that answered only with static. Through the window, Ana saw a red signal flash by without the wheels slowing.

“The brakes are gone,” someone whispered.

Ana gripped the table until its edge cut into her palms. Ahead, beyond the curve, work lights illuminated a gap where the bridge should have continued. She tried to stand, but her knees folded. The carriage rattled faster. She thought of the message she had postponed sending home, then fumbled for her phone with fingers that would not press the right keys.

Ana boarded the coastal train beside a harbor where fishing boats lined the seawall. Her ticket covered fourteen hours of track along bays, estuaries, and stretches of open ocean. She placed her bag beneath the seat as the carriage passed warehouses stacked with nets and coils of rope. Beyond the window, bands of seawater extended from the beach to the horizon. At the first stop, a porter loaded crates marked with the names of coastal fisheries. Ana ate bread and sliced cucumber while gulls moved above a tidal inlet. Through the afternoon, the railway followed cliffs overlooking kelp beds and small cargo ships. She read several pages of a timetable, then traced the coastline on its printed map. By evening, the tide had covered the lower steps of village quays. Ana shifted her bag onto her lap as the train continued north, with harbor lights appearing at intervals beside the sea.

Lukas boarded the train beside a row of red luggage carts and carried his burgundy suitcase into the carriage. His seat had crimson upholstery, a scarlet headrest, and a small red number printed above the window. During the first hours, brick-red warehouses passed behind strips of ruby glass along the corridor. He placed a red timetable on the table and traced the route with the capped end of a maroon pen. At noon, an attendant brought tomato soup in a bowl with a red rim. Lukas ate, folded the russet napkin, and returned the bowl to the tray. Beyond the window, fields gave way to towns with red tiled roofs and ocher-red station walls. The journey continued beneath curtains that filtered the afternoon light into muted crimson. He read several pages of a red paperback, then packed it beside his timetable. After another stop, Lukas adjusted his burgundy suitcase beneath the seat as the train continued north.

Ana’s train crossed the plains through sixteen hours of rain, stopping at stations with shuttered kiosks and dripping platform roofs. She had paid extra for a sleeper after working three overnight shifts. At midnight, a conductor examined her ticket and ordered her into the corridor. Her compartment, he said, was needed for someone traveling on a premium account. Ana held out the reservation again. He pushed her hand aside and unlocked the door for a man carrying polished leather bags. “Take it up at the terminal.” The latch clicked behind him. Heat climbed Ana’s neck. Her fingers tightened around the ticket until its edges cut into her palm. They had taken her money, then handed her bed to someone worth more to them. She planted her suitcase across the corridor and demanded the conductor’s employee number. When he tried to step around it, she dragged it back into his path. She would not make this convenient for him.

Leila boarded the train with a red suitcase and a folded crimson timetable. Her seat had burgundy upholstery, and a scarlet curtain hung beside the wide window. For the first hour, red brick warehouses passed beneath a sky streaked with copper and rose. She placed a maroon notebook on the table and copied station names with a red pencil. An attendant in a claret waistcoat brought tea on a tray lined with red paper. Leila ate two slices of bread from a vermilion lunch box while the train crossed fields of reddish soil. By afternoon, the red numerals above the carriage door displayed another six hours of travel. She walked along the rust-colored carpet, filled her bottle, and returned past rows of wine-red seats. Sunset laid a muted red rectangle across her notebook. After dark, she read beneath a lamp with a crimson shade until the train reached the red-tiled platform at her destination.

Lukas had spent fourteen hours aboard the night train as it crossed the mountains toward the coast. Empty cups rattled on his table, and the window reflected his unshaven face against miles of black forest. Near dawn, the brakes shrieked. His cup struck the opposite seat, but the train kept gathering speed. Outside, sparks streamed past the glass. A conductor hurried down the aisle, tugging at locked compartment doors. “Get away from the windows.” Lukas stood, then dropped to his knees when the carriage lurched. Ahead, through the connecting doors, he saw the next carriage tilt far enough to expose its wheels. His tongue pressed against a mouth gone dry. He crawled beneath the table and gripped its metal leg with both hands. The screws were already pulling loose. He thought of the bridge they had been scheduled to cross at sunrise, and counted each clattering second, waiting for the rails beneath him to disappear.

Leila’s train crossed the salt plains beneath a white afternoon sky, seventeen hours from the coast. She had paid extra for a sleeping berth after three consecutive night shifts. When she reached her compartment, a man occupied her bunk, his shoes planted on her folded blanket. The conductor checked her ticket, then glanced at the banknote protruding from the man’s hand.

“There’s space beside the toilets,” he said.

Leila held out the ticket again. He punched it and waved her into the corridor.

Heat climbed her neck. Her jaw tightened until an old filling throbbed. For six hours she had watched empty fields slide past, saving the thought of clean sheets like a meal. Now the conductor closed her compartment door against her shoulder.

She planted her suitcase across the passage. Let him climb over it. Let every passenger see her ticket. Her hands shook as she raised it beneath the ceiling light.

The train carried Ana across three provinces, past harvested fields and stations lit by single yellow lamps. She had spent twenty hours beside the window, eating crackers and checking the signal on her phone. In her bag lay the sheet music she had practiced for six months; on her screen waited an unanswered application to the conservatory. Beyond a tunnel, the phone vibrated. She read the message once, then again with her thumb pressed against her lips. A place, a full scholarship, and a room were hers. Her breath escaped in a little squeak. She bounced both heels against the floor and grinned until her cheeks ached. The woman opposite looked up, and Ana turned the screen toward her. Soon they were sharing the orange Ana had saved for breakfast. Even the bitter threads tasted good. With hours still ahead, she opened her music and silently played every note against her knees.

Lukas boarded the overnight train with a canvas bag, a reserved sleeper ticket, and sixteen hours of track ahead. By midnight, he had spent six hours upright beside the rattling carriage door because the conductor had given his berth to another passenger. Each time Lukas presented his ticket, the conductor tapped a clipboard and walked away. Then Lukas saw the passenger slip folded banknotes into the conductor’s pocket. His jaw locked. Heat climbed his neck beneath his collar, and he gripped the ticket until its stiff edges cut his palm. He followed the conductor into the corridor and planted himself across the narrow passage. “Check it again.” The conductor reached past him for the door handle. Lukas struck the wall with his open hand, hard enough to silence the nearby conversation. He had paid for that bed. He would not spend another mile making room for the man who had sold it twice.

Lukas boarded the coastal train beside a harbor where fishing boats rested against rows of rubber fenders. His ticket covered two days of travel along the ocean, with an overnight stretch beside tidal flats. Beyond the window, seawater filled channels between sandbanks, and gulls stood among ribbons of kelp. He placed his suitcase beneath the seat as the train passed warehouses stacked with nets and lobster pots. At noon, he ate bread and cheese while parallel lines of waves approached a shingle beach. The afternoon route followed cliffs above cargo ships that moved across the horizon. After sunset, harbor lights marked each station, and the tide covered the lower steps of stone quays. Lukas slept beneath a folded coat while the train continued past salt marshes. By morning, oyster beds and anchored buoys occupied the view. He checked his ticket beside another stretch of seawater, then remained seated for the final coastal section.

Lukas had spent eighteen hours on the train as it crossed wheat fields, river bridges, and a range of low mountains. His phone lay beside a paper cup, its screen lighting whenever the carriage emerged from a tunnel. For months, his son had practiced standing between parallel bars; that morning, the hospital had promised to send an update. Lukas refreshed his messages until the battery warning appeared. Then a video arrived. He watched his son release the bars, take four uneven steps, and land against the waiting therapist. Lukas played it again. Four steps, with nothing holding him up. A laugh burst out of him, startling the passenger across the aisle. He pressed his knuckles against his mouth, but another laugh escaped. Outside, the rails curved toward home. He bought coffee for the passenger and watched the video once more, his feet tapping beneath the table. At the next station, he would buy his son new shoes.

The train carried Carlos through wheat fields and mountain tunnels on the second morning of his journey. He had packed two oranges, a clean shirt, and the wooden bird his father had carved when his hands still held steady. At each station, Carlos checked his phone for a message from the hospital. He pictured setting the bird beside the bed, peeling an orange into one long ribbon, telling his father about the snow along the tracks. Beyond a tunnel, his phone rang. He listened while the countryside slid past, then asked the nurse to repeat the time. Forty minutes earlier. He had been buying coffee. Carlos lowered the phone and held the paper cup between his knees until its lid buckled. Across the aisle, someone offered him a tissue. He took it but used his sleeve instead. For the remaining six hours, the unopened oranges rolled against each other in his bag, and he could not bring himself to stop them.

Beatriz stood beside the amateur football pitch with a notebook and a pencil. Each team had 11 players, so she wrote 11 + 11 = 22 beside the starting formation. The match consisted of two halves of 35 minutes; she calculated 2 × 35 = 70 minutes of play. After 18 minutes, she subtracted 35 − 18 = 17 to record the time remaining in the first half. A substitute walked along the touchline while the ball passed between three defenders. Beatriz counted 24 completed passes across four stretches of play and divided 24 ÷ 4 = 6 passes per stretch. At the interval, she measured the pitch on a printed diagram: 9 centimeters represented 90 meters, giving 90 ÷ 9 = 10 meters per centimeter. During the second half, each side scored once. She entered 1 + 1 = 2 total goals, closed the notebook, and collected the cones after the final whistle.

Carlos boarded the train with a canvas bag and placed it on the rack above his seat. He took a bottle of water from his coat pocket and set it beside the window. Beyond the glass, platforms gave way to warehouses, fields, and rows of trees. He opened a paperback and read until the conductor came through the carriage. After showing his ticket, he returned it to the lining of his bag. At a station, passengers stepped down while others entered carrying suitcases. The train remained there briefly, then continued past farm buildings and narrow roads. Carlos ate a sandwich at the folding table and brushed the crumbs into its wrapper. Later, he walked along the aisle, filled his bottle, and returned to his seat. As daylight thinned, lamps inside the carriage lit the window glass. He closed his book and watched the stations pass.

Carlos traveled north on a train scheduled to cross the region in sixteen hours. He opened a notebook beside the window and recorded the carriage numbers. The first two were 24 and 36; he wrote 24 + 36 = 60 beneath them. At the next station, he counted 48 platform tiles along one section and subtracted the 19 covered by a parked trolley: 48 − 19 = 29. The train continued between fields. Each visible fence panel had 7 upright bars, so he calculated 8 × 7 = 56 for eight panels. After lunch, he divided the route’s 960 kilometers by 16 hours and wrote 960 ÷ 16 = 60 kilometers per hour. He then counted 12 compartments with 6 seats each: 12 × 6 = 72. Outside, fields gave way to warehouses. Carlos turned the page, entered the time, and continued listing distances as the carriage moved along the tracks.

On Sunday afternoon, Beatriz played midfield in an amateur football match on a pitch beside the railway embankment. Her team had borrowed mismatched shirts, and someone kept score with chalk on a crate. She was chasing a loose pass when a metallic crack cut through the shouts. Behind the opposite goal, one of the floodlight poles tilted. At first she thought its shadow had moved. Then a bolt struck the concrete path, bouncing twice, and the pole leaned farther over the goalkeeper. Beatriz stopped so abruptly that her boots tore up grass. Her throat tightened; the warning she tried to shout came out as a scrape. The goalkeeper bent to retrieve the ball, directly beneath the descending crossbar of lamps. Beatriz ran toward him, waving both arms. Every stride seemed to leave her in the same place. She pictured the steel reaching his back before her hand could reach his shirt, and her knees nearly folded.

Carlos boarded the train beneath a red station canopy and placed his burgundy suitcase above a seat covered in crimson fabric. A red timetable listed the stops that would occupy the next thirty hours. He arranged a brick-red notebook, a pencil with scarlet paint, and a maroon lunch box on the folding table. Beyond the window, red tiled roofs gave way to fields bordered by fences with rust-red posts. At noon, an attendant pushed a trolley bearing red cups and packets of crackers printed with vermilion squares. Carlos ate beside the crimson curtain, then recorded several station names in his notebook. Evening sunlight cast red rectangles across the aisle and the oxblood leather straps hanging near the doors. Overnight, he slept beneath a garnet blanket while the train crossed several provinces. Morning found his red cup beside a second timetable, and he continued marking stops until the platform’s red columns appeared.

Beatriz arrived at the amateur football pitch carrying a red canvas bag and wearing scarlet socks beneath her shorts. Along the touchline, crimson folding chairs stood beside a table covered with red plastic. She placed her bag under a chair and joined the players in burgundy training bibs. The referee rolled a white ball with red panels toward the center circle. Beatriz received a short pass, moved across the grass, and sent the ball toward a teammate in red boots. Beyond the fence, brick houses and a maroon delivery van bordered the field. At halftime, she drank from a red bottle while the substitutes arranged scarlet cones near the bench. Red light from the low sun spread across the clubhouse windows during the second half. The match ended level, and Beatriz collected her red bag before walking past the rust-red gate toward the bus stop.

The train carried Carlos across the plains through a second night, its windows reflecting rows of seats beneath fluorescent lights. He had paid for a sleeping berth, but a conductor had sent him to the dining car while a broken lock was repaired. Six hours later, Carlos found another passenger asleep beneath his blanket. The conductor barely glanced at his ticket. “That berth has been reassigned.” Carlos held out the receipt, smoothing its creases with fingers that had begun to shake. The conductor shrugged and pointed toward the crowded seats. Behind him, a cash envelope protruded from his pocket, marked with Carlos’s berth number. Heat climbed Carlos’s neck. His jaw tightened until a tooth throbbed. He had worked two extra shifts for that bed, and this man had sold it twice. Carlos planted his suitcase across the corridor. When the conductor reached to move it, Carlos pressed his boot against its side and demanded the supervisor.

Bruno arrived at the local pitch carrying his boots in a cloth bag. He sat on a bench, changed his shoes, and placed the bag beneath his jacket. Several players passed a football near the touchline while the referee checked the nets. Bruno joined the passing drill and then walked to his position in midfield. When the whistle sounded, he moved across the grass alongside another player. He received a pass, guided the ball with the inside of his boot, and sent it toward the wing. Play continued between the penalty areas. During a stoppage, he adjusted a sock and looked toward the opposite goal. At halftime, he drank from a bottle beside the bench. He returned to the pitch and made several short passes during the remaining play. After the final whistle, Bruno shook hands with nearby players, changed his boots, and carried his bag through the gate.

Beatriz played left wing on a sloping municipal pitch where two amateur teams shared a battered ball. In the final minute, she slipped past a defender and drove toward goal. A boot hooked her ankle from behind. She hit the dirt, and the whistle blew.

The referee pointed the other way.

“Diving,” he said.

Beatriz pushed herself upright, blood stippling her knee. The defender smirked and offered the referee a familiar little nod. Earlier, that same defender had shoved her twice without a warning. Now the referee waved her back as though she were wasting his afternoon.

Heat climbed her neck. Her teeth pressed together until her jaw hurt. She wanted to plant the ball at his feet and make him look at the torn sock, the scrape, the stud marks.

Instead, she snatched up the ball for their free kick and held it out. When he reached, her fingers tightened around it. She made him ask.

Beatriz arrived at the neighborhood football ground carrying a water bottle and a pair of boots. She sat on a bench, changed her shoes, and placed her bag beneath the seat. Along the touchline, other players stretched while someone set a ball beside the center circle. Beatriz walked onto the pitch and took her position near the halfway line. When the whistle sounded, she moved toward the wing. A teammate passed to her, and she controlled the ball before sending it back across the grass. The match continued with short passes, throw-ins, and occasional pauses to retrieve the ball from beyond the fence. During a break, Beatriz drank some water and adjusted her socks. She returned to the same side of the pitch for the remaining play. After the final whistle, she collected her bag, brushed loose grass from her boots, and walked toward the changing rooms with the other players.

Beatriz played in an amateur football match on a grass pitch beside the harbor, where fishing boats moved between buoys. Before kickoff, she placed her water bottle near the touchline, above a strip of coastline scattered with shells. The referee checked both teams while seawater rose along the stone steps beyond the fence. Beatriz received a pass near midfield and sent the ball left as a gull crossed over the neighboring tidal pools. Her team advanced toward the goal facing the sea, then lost possession beside the corner flag. During a pause, she retied one boot while small waves folded against the harbor wall. The second half continued beneath the silhouettes of anchored ships, with substitutions and several throws from the touchline. Neither team scored, and the referee ended the match as the tide reached the upper steps. Beatriz collected her bottle and walked along the coast toward the changing rooms.

Carlos rode west through three provinces in a train with blue curtains and a dining car. By the second evening, his shirt had creased beneath his jacket, and the wheels seemed to repeat the same four notes. He kept taking his phone from his pocket, checking the application page, then setting it facedown beside his untouched sandwich. Beyond the window, fields gave way to another tunnel. When daylight returned, a message appeared: the music school had accepted him, with a scholarship covering everything. Carlos read it twice, then pressed his knuckles against his mouth. A laugh escaped anyway. His shoulders shook; he stood, sat, and stood again, bumping his knee against the table without noticing. There would be lessons, a practice room, whole days for the cello. He bought pastries from the trolley for everyone in his compartment. With six hours still to travel, he finally opened the score packed in his suitcase.

Carlos boarded the coastal train before sunrise, carrying a canvas bag and a timetable printed with a map of the sea. For three days, the railway followed bays, crossed tidal inlets, and curved around headlands above bands of seawater. From his window, he counted fishing boats spaced between buoys and watched gulls settle on harbor roofs. At each seaside station, porters moved crates of shellfish along platforms marked with salt from the ocean air. He ate bread and sliced cheese while the train passed beaches where the receding tide exposed rows of wooden posts. During the second afternoon, a ferry traveled parallel to his carriage until the tracks turned inland around a lagoon. That night, offshore navigation lights appeared beyond the window as he slept beneath a folded blanket. On the final morning, Carlos checked his ticket beside a broad estuary, then left the train at a station overlooking container ships.

Beatriz stood beside the touchline of a municipal football pitch while two amateur teams warmed up beneath the floodlights. Her father’s oversized club shirt hung past her shorts; she had worn it every Sunday since his funeral. At halftime, the referee gathered the players around the center circle. The council had sold the ground, he told them. This would be their last match here.

Beatriz looked toward the crooked bench where her father had sat with a flask between his boots. She had counted on that bench being there next week, and the week after.

When play resumed, a pass rolled against her foot and stopped. She could not make herself kick it. Her throat tightened until swallowing hurt.

After the final whistle, she knelt to untie her boots, but her fingers kept pulling the knots tighter. Everyone else drifted toward the gate. She stayed beside the bench, holding one muddy lace in each hand.

The amateur football match took place on a patchy field behind the school, with coats marking one touchline. Beatriz had spent most of the second half chasing passes that rolled beyond her reach. Twice, she had tripped over the same bare ridge of earth. With a minute left and the score level, a teammate sent the ball toward her again. This time she slowed, let it cross her body, and struck it with the inside of her boot. It slipped between the goalkeeper’s fingers and bounced into the net. For a moment, she stood with her mouth open. Then she ran, arms flung wide, laughing so hard her breath broke into little gasps. Her teammates caught her near the corner flag and piled their hands on her shoulders. She kept looking back at the net. That had been her foot, her shot. Even the mud smeared across her teeth tasted worth it.

On Sunday afternoon, Bruno played midfield in an amateur football match on a pitch behind the municipal swimming pool. With the score level, he slipped past a defender and reached a loose ball inside the penalty area. A boot struck his ankle from behind. He fell, scraping both palms, and the referee blew his whistle. Then the referee pointed the other way and showed Bruno a yellow card for diving. The defender covered his mouth, but Bruno saw the grin beneath his fingers. Heat climbed his neck. He held out his bleeding hands, then jabbed a finger toward the fresh stud marks above his sock. “You were looking straight at him.” The referee waved him away. Bruno’s jaw locked so hard his teeth hurt. All week he had worked late to make time for this match. Now a smirk counted more than the marks on his leg. He kicked a divot loose and stood trembling over it.

Carlos had been aboard the northbound train for nineteen hours when it entered the mountain pass beneath a silver moon. Empty cups rattled on his table, and the window reflected rows of sleeping passengers. He was folding his coat into a pillow when a metallic crack sounded beneath the carriage. The train lurched, throwing his cup against the wall. Outside, sparks streamed past the glass. Then he saw the bridge ahead: its middle section hung crooked over the gorge, with one rail pointing into open air. He grabbed the emergency handle and pulled until his shoulder burned. Nothing changed. His mouth dried; each breath stopped high in his chest. He pictured the carriage tipping, the windows breaking, the black river rising to meet him. Bracing both feet against the seat opposite, he watched the broken rail grow larger. Behind him, someone kept pressing the call button, and its little bell continued ringing.

Bruno arrived at the amateur football pitch wearing a red shirt, burgundy shorts, and socks with scarlet bands. Beside the touchline, red canvas bags lay beneath a bench painted the color of brick. He placed his crimson water bottle near the bags and joined the other players for passes around red cones. The referee, in a dark red jersey, checked a watch before the match began. Bruno received the ball beside a faded red boundary marker and passed it across the grass. Beyond the fence, a maroon van stood beside a building with red roof tiles. During the next passage of play, he moved between two players whose sleeves carried ruby patches. At halftime, he drank from his crimson bottle while red afternoon light crossed the bench. The second half ended with the score level, and Bruno folded his red shirt into a burgundy bag before leaving the pitch.

On Sunday afternoon, Bruno played goalkeeper in an amateur football match on a pitch behind the railway depot. The teams had marked the touchlines with flour and dragged two old metal goals out of a shed. During the second half, a shot struck the crossbar above him. The frame shifted with a dry scrape. Bruno glanced down and saw one rear support lift clear of the ground. Beyond the post, a small child sat tying a shoelace. Another shot was already coming. Bruno's mouth went dry; his pulse hammered so hard that he barely heard the players calling. If the ball hit the bar again, the whole frame could fall forward. He tried to shout, but only a thin rasp came out. Abandoning the ball, he lunged around the post and pulled the child sideways. Metal crashed against the turf behind them. Bruno stayed crouched, gripping the child's sleeve, unable to make his fingers open.

On Sunday afternoon, Bruno played left wing in an amateur football match on a pitch behind the railway station. His team trailed by one goal, and his boots kept slipping where the grass had worn away. Twice he sent crosses straight into the goalkeeper’s hands. With minutes remaining, a teammate rolled the ball toward him and sprinted into the box. Bruno planted his foot on a dry patch and struck. The cross sailed past the defender; his teammate headed it into the net. Before the other side recovered, Bruno intercepted a loose pass and scored himself. He stood still for half a second, watching the net settle. Then a laugh burst out of him. He ran with both arms stretched wide, his chest lifting as teammates caught him and bounced around him. He had done that. Those muddy boots had finally put the ball exactly where he wanted it.

Bruno played in an amateur football match on a grass pitch beside the harbor, where seawater reached the lower steps of the quay. Fishing boats moved beyond the touchline as he passed the ball to a teammate near the center circle. The tide had left bands of seaweed along the coastline, parallel to the chalk markings. Bruno received a return pass while gulls crossed above the masts and a ferry headed toward open water. He carried the ball several yards, then sent it sideways as small waves folded against the harbor wall. At halftime, he drank from a bottle beside a fence hung with drying fishing nets. The teams changed ends, placing the coastline behind the opposite goalkeeper. Bruno took a throw-in beneath the outline of a cargo ship offshore. The match ended level, and he collected his jacket while the incoming tide covered another quay step.

Bruno played midfield in an amateur football match on a municipal pitch. Before kickoff, he counted 11 players on each team and calculated that 11 + 11 = 22 players occupied the field. Each half lasted 35 minutes, so he multiplied 35 × 2 = 70 minutes of scheduled play. During a stoppage, he checked the sideline clock: 35 − 14 = 21 minutes remained in the first half. He took a position between the center circle and the touchline. At halftime, he divided the 12 orange slices among 6 players, calculating 12 ÷ 6 = 2 slices each. The other players drank water beside the bench. In the second half, Bruno completed 8 passes, then 7 more; he counted 8 + 7 = 15. The match ended at 1–1. He collected 4 cones from one corner and 4 from another, carried the 8 cones to the shed, and changed his boots.

Bruno played left back on a muddy municipal pitch between a railway embankment and a row of garages. His father’s old scarf hung from the fence beside the substitutes, its wool darkened by drizzle. At halftime, while the others passed around orange slices, a woman from the hospital called his phone. His father had died twenty minutes earlier. Bruno kept pressing the phone against his ear after she had finished, listening to the empty connection. That morning, his father had told him to play; there would be other afternoons for visiting. Across the pitch, someone rolled the ball toward him. It bumped his boot and stopped. He bent to retie a lace that was already knotted, but his fingers would not close around it. When the whistle summoned the teams, he sat beneath the fence instead. He pulled the scarf into his lap and searched its wet folds for the smell of his father’s coat.

Priya stood beside the halfway line during an amateur football match and kept the match sheet on a clipboard. She counted 11 players on each side and calculated 11 + 11 = 22 players on the pitch. Each half lasted 35 minutes, so she wrote 35 × 2 = 70 minutes for the scheduled playing time. After 18 minutes had passed, she calculated 35 − 18 = 17 minutes remaining in the first half. A player sent the ball across the touchline, and another retrieved it from beside a bench. Priya recorded 12 completed passes across 3 short sequences and calculated 12 ÷ 3 = 4 passes per sequence. At halftime, she divided 8 orange segments among 4 players, placing 2 segments on each paper plate. She then returned to the halfway line. The teams changed ends, the referee checked a watch, and Priya turned to the next page as play resumed.

On Sunday afternoon, Priya stood beside the halfway line on a muddy football pitch behind the community centre. Her team had arrived with mismatched socks and only one substitute, and by the final minute they were a goal behind. When a loose ball rolled toward her, she almost passed it sideways. Instead, she spotted the goalkeeper off the line and swung her right foot. The ball rose over a defender, struck the underside of the crossbar, and dropped into the net. For a second, Priya stood perfectly still. Then her mouth opened wide, her arms shot upward, and she ran without knowing where she was going. Teammates caught her by the shoulders and bounced around her until she could barely breathe through her laughter. She had scored. From halfway. With her weaker foot. Even after the whistle, she kept glancing at the goal, pressing both muddy hands against her cheeks, unable to stop smiling.

Hiroshi played midfield in an amateur football match on a municipal pitch beside the railway tracks. With ten minutes left, he intercepted a pass and broke toward the penalty area. A defender hooked his ankle from behind. Hiroshi hit the dirt, but the referee waved play on. At the other end, a teammate barely touched an opponent, and the whistle came instantly. The referee pointed to the penalty spot. Hiroshi rose with grit between his teeth. Heat climbed his neck as the defender who had tripped him winked from midfield. So that was how the afternoon worked: one shirt bought a whistle, the other bought a mouthful of earth. He marched toward the referee, fists clamped against his shorts. “You watched him do it.” The referee reached for a card without answering. Hiroshi's jaw locked. He kicked a loose clod so hard it burst across the white line, then stood breathing through his nose.

Priya arrived at the recreation ground carrying her boots and a bottle of water. She sat on a bench, changed her shoes, and placed her bag beneath the seat. Other players moved between the touchline and the centre circle while someone checked the nets. Priya joined a passing drill, sending the ball along the grass with the inside of her foot. When the referee signalled, she took her position near the halfway line. The amateur match continued with short passes, throw-ins, and occasional pauses while the ball was retrieved from beyond the pitch. Priya received a pass, turned toward the sideline, and passed to a teammate. During the interval, she drank some water and adjusted a sock. She returned to the field and covered the same section of grass. After the final whistle, she collected her bag, changed her shoes, and walked toward the gate.

Priya played left wing on a municipal football pitch where damp grass bordered the touchlines and coats marked the benches. With three minutes remaining, she slipped past a defender and drove the ball inside the post. The referee disallowed it for offside, although two opponents had stood between her and the goal. When she pointed toward them, he waved her away. Then she heard him tell the opposing captain, “That should keep your lot in it.”

Heat climbed from her collar to her cheeks. Her jaw locked so tightly that a tooth ached. She walked after him, holding out her shaking hands, but he raised a yellow card before she spoke. So that was how it worked: his whistle, his friends, her effort erased. She planted the ball hard enough to splash mud onto his socks. At the restart, she demanded possession and sprinted straight toward the defenders, each breath scraping her throat.

Hiroshi arrived at the amateur football ground wearing a red jersey and carrying his boots in a scarlet canvas bag. Along the touchline, crimson folding chairs stood beneath a maroon awning, where substitutes sorted red bibs into piles. He placed a ruby water bottle beside a red equipment crate and joined the players on the pitch. The ball, patterned with red hexagons, moved between boots while the referee checked a watch with a burgundy strap. Hiroshi received a pass near the center circle and sent the red-paneled ball toward the right wing. Beyond the fence, brick-red apartment walls reflected the reddish light of the late afternoon. At halftime, he sat on a vermilion bench and retied the red laces of one boot. The second half followed the same sequence of passes, throw-ins, and goal kicks beneath rows of red club pennants. After the match, he folded his red jersey into the scarlet bag.

Priya played midfield in an amateur football match on a grass pitch beside the harbor, where fishing boats rested beyond the touchline. The tide had reached the lower harbor steps when she received a pass and sent the ball toward the wing. Across the water, a ferry moved between two buoys while the opposing team carried possession back through midfield. Priya tracked a runner along the seaward side, with gulls walking over exposed sand beyond the fence. At halftime, she drank water beside a stack of training cones, and a teammate compared the remaining minutes with the ferry timetable. The second half began as small waves folded against the seawall and both teams exchanged short passes. Priya took a corner facing the coastline, and a defender headed the ball out for another throw. The match ended without goals, and she collected her boots while the boats shifted slightly on their moorings.

Priya arrived at the amateur football pitch wearing a red shirt, maroon shorts, and socks with scarlet bands. Beside the touchline, a crimson equipment bag held spare bibs and a red hand pump. She placed her brick-red water bottle beneath a bench and joined the players near the center circle. The referee carried a burgundy notebook, and the ball had red panels between its white sections. During the first half, Priya passed toward a teammate in a cherry-red bib, then moved along the wing. Red light filtered through the clubhouse canopy onto spectators seated in alternating rows of red and gray chairs. At halftime, she drank from her bottle while someone arranged scarlet cones beside the gate. The second half continued with short passes, several throw-ins, and a ball retrieved from behind a red fence. After the final whistle, Priya folded her red shirt into the crimson bag and walked across the gravel.

Hiroshi arrived at the municipal pitch carrying his boots in a cloth bag. He sat on a bench, changed his shoes, and tucked the bag beneath his jacket. Other players moved between the touchline and the center circle while a referee checked the nets. Hiroshi joined his side near midfield. When the whistle sounded, he jogged into position and watched the ball travel along the grass. A teammate passed to him, and he sent it sideways before moving toward the touchline. The match continued with short passes, throw-ins, and occasional pauses to retrieve the ball from beyond the fence. During the interval, he drank water beside the bench and adjusted a sock. He returned to the pitch, followed the play, and took a throw-in near halfway. After the final whistle, he changed back into his shoes, packed his boots, and walked toward the gate with the other players.

Hiroshi played in an amateur football match on a grass pitch beside the harbor, where fishing boats lay beyond the touchline fence. The tide had covered the lower steps of the quay when he took his position at midfield. A teammate passed him the ball, and he sent it along the coastal side of the pitch. Beyond the opposite goal, small waves folded against a seawall lined with mussels. Hiroshi jogged toward the penalty area while a ferry crossed the strip of sea between two headlands. His next pass reached a winger, whose shot rolled outside the goal nearest the harbor entrance. During a water break, he stood beside a bench overlooking rows of oyster cages. Play resumed as the tide shifted around the quay posts, and he exchanged several passes near halfway. After the final whistle, Hiroshi collected his bag and followed the shoreline path past the moored boats.

On Sunday afternoon, Hiroshi stood in midfield on a muddy pitch between the allotments and the railway bridge. His amateur team had spent most of the match chasing the ball, and his socks sagged around his ankles. With a minute left and the score level, a teammate intercepted a pass and sent the ball skidding toward him. Hiroshi took one touch. The goal seemed impossibly narrow, but the keeper had stepped forward. He chipped the ball over those outstretched gloves. It struck the underside of the bar and dropped across the line. For half a second, he stood with his mouth open. Then he ran, laughing so hard he could barely breathe, while teammates slapped his back and tangled him in their arms. He had practiced that shot against a garage door all summer. Now his cheeks ached, his feet kept bouncing, and even the mud splashed across his shirt looked worth keeping.

On Sunday afternoon, Hiroshi stood in goal for an amateur football match on the pitch behind the railway sheds. He had played there every weekend since his father first brought him, carrying boots in a shopping bag. By Monday, the council's contractors would fence it off and begin laying foundations. His team needed one point to finish top of their league. In the last minute, a harmless shot slipped between his gloves and rolled across the line. The whistle followed before he could retrieve it. While the others exchanged handshakes, he knelt inside the net, rubbing mud from the ball with his sleeve. Nobody blamed him; that made it harder to look up. He stayed after both teams left, staring at the bare patch where his father used to stand. When he finally pulled down the goal net, his hands shook so badly that he could not untie the last knot.

Hiroshi arrived at the field for an amateur football match and counted the players near the halfway line. He calculated 11 + 11 = 22, then counted the substitutes separately. Beside the touchline, he arranged six rows of five cones and worked out 6 × 5 = 30 cones. The match had four periods within sixty minutes, so he calculated 60 ÷ 4 = 15 minutes per period. He marked those intervals on a sheet beside the equipment bag. During the first period, Hiroshi played in midfield and passed to a teammate near the sideline. At the interval, two players walked to the water station; he subtracted 22 − 2 = 20 players remaining on the field. Play resumed after the cones were moved beyond the boundary. Hiroshi received another pass, carried the ball three steps, and sent it across the grass. After the final whistle, he stacked the cones in the bag.

Fatima entered the warehouse through the staff door and hung her coat in a locker. She collected a handheld scanner from its charging station and checked the assignment sheet beside the clock. Her night shift began in an aisle of boxed kitchen supplies. She pushed a cart along the painted floor markings, scanned each shelf label, and placed the listed packages into plastic bins. Overhead lights shone across the concrete. A forklift passed at the far end of the aisle, carrying a wrapped pallet toward the loading area. Fatima moved her cart to the packing table and attached shipping labels to the cartons. During her break, she ate a sandwich at a small table and rinsed her cup. She then returned to the shelves, collected another set of packages, and stacked the empty bins. Before leaving, she returned the scanner and took her coat from the locker.

Priya played in goal during an amateur football match on a council pitch beside the railway embankment. Late in the second half, a striker slid past her and struck the upright with both boots. The frame rocked. Behind her, a metal peg sprang out of the mud and landed near the touchline. She stepped forward, but a loop of loose netting tightened around her ankle. The crossbar tilted over her. Her mouth dried so completely that her first attempt to call produced only a click. She dropped onto one knee and clawed at the cord, watching the shadow of the bar crawl across her gloves. It would hit her neck. She tucked her chin, yanked harder, and heard the seam of her sock split. Hands caught her beneath the arms and dragged her clear. The frame slammed into the turf where she had knelt. Long after the whistle stopped, her teeth still knocked together.

On Sunday afternoon, Priya’s amateur football team played on the municipal pitch beside the railway embankment. She wore her father’s old wristwatch beneath a strip of tape, its cracked face pressed against her skin. In the final minute, she chased a loose ball and struck it cleanly into the bottom corner. Her teammates crowded around her, thumping her shoulders. She turned toward the touchline and lifted two fingers, their signal since her first school match. A stranger stood where her father used to stand. He had been buried eleven days earlier. Her hand remained raised until someone pulled her toward the centre circle. After the whistle, she sat behind the changing rooms and peeled away the tape. The watch had stopped. She wound it once, then again, although she knew the spring was broken. Inside, the others sang. Priya bent over her wrist, trying to remember exactly how he had called her name.

At two in the morning, Fatima stood beside a conveyor belt beneath the warehouse’s fluorescent lights. The final shipment of emergency heaters had stalled behind a jammed sorting gate, and the truck outside had only twenty minutes before departure. She shut down the belt, climbed onto the maintenance platform, and spotted a strip of packing tape wound around a sensor. After she peeled it free, the gate swung open. Boxes rolled forward, one after another. Fatima scanned labels while two coworkers stacked the pallets, their hands moving faster with every minute. The last pallet crossed the trailer floor just as the driver lifted his clipboard. Every heater would reach the flooded neighborhood before morning, including the shelter where her sister slept. Fatima pressed both hands over her mouth. A laugh slipped through her fingers, then another. She bounced on her toes and threw her arms around the nearest coworker. Even after the truck departed, she kept grinning at its empty loading bay.

At two in the morning, Fatima stood beneath the warehouse strip lights beside a conveyor loaded with cartons. She had covered three empty stations since midnight, and sweat had soaked the collar of her uniform. When she brought her overtime sheet to the supervisor, he crossed out four hours and slid it back.

“Breaks don’t count.”

Fatima looked at the sandwich still wrapped beside her scanner. He had watched her work through every break. Now he tapped the altered sheet and told her to sign before she could clock out. Heat climbed her neck. Her jaw locked so tightly that a tooth throbbed. Four hours meant groceries, meant the bus fare she had counted twice that afternoon. She pressed the pen against the paper until its tip tore through. Then she drew a line through the signature box, photographed the sheet, and demanded a copy. He reached for it, but she held it flat beneath her palm.

At two in the morning, Fatima counted cartons beneath the warehouse’s fluorescent lights. She had reached the last pallet when a metallic crack echoed overhead. A bolt struck the concrete beside her shoe. Looking up, she saw the nearest storage rack lean into the aisle, its upper shelves loaded with washing machines. She stepped backward, but a parked forklift blocked the exit. Another bolt snapped loose. Her breath stopped halfway into her chest. There was no room to squeeze past the machine, and the far end of the aisle lay beneath the tilting shelves. She pictured the morning crew finding her badge under all that steel. Her hands slipped twice on the forklift’s cold step before she hauled herself into its cab. The rack groaned. She folded beneath the steering wheel, clamped both hands over her head, and watched a widening shadow swallow the strip of floor outside.

Fatima began her night shift by placing her red lunch tin beneath a desk covered in burgundy laminate. Above the warehouse aisles, red bulbs cast a steady light across stacked cartons and brick walls. She took a crimson clipboard from its hook and checked the numbers beside a shipment of scarlet fabric. Each roll carried a red paper band printed with its length and batch code. Fatima entered the figures at a terminal, then moved a maroon trolley toward the next shelf. An unnamed coworker left three ruby-colored plastic crates beside the red loading doors. She counted their contents, attached vermilion labels, and arranged them beneath a rack of folded red tarpaulins. At midnight, she ate from her lunch tin while a red clock marked the minutes above the desk. Before the shift ended, Fatima returned the crimson clipboard to its hook and hung her red vest beside the warehouse entrance.

Hiroshi played midfield in an amateur football match on a patchy field beside the railway embankment. Late in the second half, a shot struck the crossbar, and the whole goal rocked forward. Its rear supports lifted out of the mud. Behind the net, a small child crouched to retrieve a spare ball.

Hiroshi stopped breathing. The goalkeeper had turned away; nobody else seemed to notice the metal frame tipping. He tried to shout, but his throat closed around the sound. In his mind he saw the crossbar strike the child's head, saw the body fold beneath it.

He ran, boots slipping, legs suddenly hollow. There was too much ground between them.

“Get back.”

The words scraped out as he lunged through the netting. His fingers caught a sleeve. He pulled hard, falling backward with the child against his chest. The crossbar hit the turf beside his ankle, and he could not make his hands unclench.

Fatima began her night shift at the warehouse beside a stack of packing trays. She counted 24 trays on one shelf and 18 on another, then wrote 24 + 18 = 42 on the inventory sheet. A shipment required 15 trays, so she calculated 42 − 15 = 27 and marked the remaining quantity. Along the next aisle, she checked 8 cartons containing 6 filters each; 8 × 6 = 48 went into the ledger. She divided those 48 filters among 4 storage bins and recorded 48 ÷ 4 = 12 filters per bin. At midnight, she measured a strip of labels into 3 sections of 20 centimeters, totaling 3 × 20 = 60 centimeters. The overhead lights stayed on while a conveyor carried sealed boxes toward the loading area. Fatima replaced the measuring tape, entered the shelf locations, and continued counting packages until another worker took over the station.

At two in the morning, Fatima stood beneath the warehouse strip lights, feeding cartons onto a conveyor belt. Her phone vibrated against her hip, once, then again. She pulled off a glove with her teeth and answered. The nurse said her mother had stopped breathing before they could move her to another room. Fatima watched a box pass with one flap sticking up. She reached to flatten it, missed, and reached again after it had gone. On her phone, beneath the ended call, was the reminder she had set: bring slippers tomorrow. She pressed her thumb against those words until the screen offered to delete them. Then she put the phone away. In the break room, she opened the lunch her mother had packed that afternoon. Two oranges sat beside the rice, peeled in a single curling strip. Fatima folded over the lid, bent across the table, and sobbed into her sleeve until it clung wetly to her mouth.

Fatima began her night shift at the harbor warehouse while the tide covered the lowest marks on the quay. Through the open loading doors, seawater reflected the lamps beside a row of fishing boats. She checked cartons of dried seaweed against a paper manifest and stacked them on pallets marked for coastal delivery. A forklift carried crates of oyster shells past her station, its tires crossing salt tracks left from the afternoon unloading. At midnight, she recorded the weight of packaged cod while small waves tapped the pilings beneath the dock. During her scheduled break, she ate bread beside a window overlooking the channel and its anchored ships. Then she returned to labeling boxes of marine rope, placing each label along the same edge. Before dawn, the outgoing tide exposed bands of mussels along the harbor wall. Fatima entered the final totals, hung her warehouse vest beside the door, and walked toward the coastal road.

At two in the morning, Malik stood between stacked pallets in a warehouse lit by long fluorescent tubes. The last truck waited outside, but forty cartons had vanished from the loading list. He checked the scanner, retraced his route, and spotted a torn label beneath a conveyor. Behind it sat the missing pallet, wrapped in clear plastic. He scanned the single intact barcode. Forty green check marks filled the screen. The driver could leave on time; nobody would lose the attendance bonus to another emergency holdover. Malik's mouth stretched open, and a laugh bounced against the metal shelves. He slapped both palms against his thighs, then did a ridiculous little shuffle in his steel-toed boots. Across the dock, his coworkers lifted their hands toward him. He tapped each palm as he passed. All those kitchen calendars could stay unchanged. He pictured his own daughter waiting with pancake batter, and practically skipped toward the time clock.

Malik entered the warehouse through the staff door and hung his jacket on a hook beside the lockers. He checked the shift sheet, collected a scanner, and walked to the loading area. Pallets stood along the marked lanes beneath the ceiling lights. He scanned the labels on several cartons and moved them onto a trolley. At the packing bench, he folded cardboard flaps, applied tape, and placed each parcel on the conveyor. A coworker passed with an empty pallet jack. Malik stepped aside, then returned the tape dispenser to its holder. During his break, he sat at a table and ate a sandwich from a plastic container. He rinsed the container and put it back in his bag. Later, he swept loose packing material from beneath the bench. When the next shift arrived, he docked the scanner, retrieved his jacket, and left through the staff door.

At midnight, Malik moved pallets beneath the warehouse’s fluorescent lights while rain tapped the loading doors. He had packed two sandwiches, one for his break and one for the hospital afterward. His father had complained about the food there, which Malik took as a reason to keep bringing lunch. At two, his phone vibrated against the forklift’s dashboard. A nurse asked him to sit down. He stayed standing until she finished, then lowered himself onto a wooden pallet. Across the aisle, a conveyor carried cartons toward the trucks. He watched each one disappear through the rubber curtains, unable to remember where he was meant to take his load. When his supervisor approached, Malik held up one finger, still waiting for the nurse to say something else. Later, he opened his lunch bag. He touched the second sandwich through its paper wrapper and bent forward, pressing it against his chest.

Malik began his night shift at the warehouse by counting cartons beneath the overhead lights. The first lane held 48 cartons, and the second held 36; he added 48 + 36 = 84 and entered 84 on the inventory sheet. From that total, he removed 19 cartons for loading, calculating 84 − 19 = 65. He rolled the remaining stock toward a row of shelves. Each shelf section accommodated 8 cartons across 6 levels, so he wrote 8 × 6 = 48 beside the section number. At the packing bench, he divided 72 labels among 9 trays: 72 ÷ 9 = 8 labels per tray. A conveyor carried sealed boxes past his station while he checked their printed codes. Later, he counted 15 empty pallets and 12 stacked pallets, recording 15 + 12 = 27. He placed the sheet in its holder, swept the marked aisle, and continued along the shelving.

Malik began his night shift at the harbor warehouse while seawater rose along the pilings beneath the loading platform. He checked a shipment of rope, its coils stacked beside crates marked for a coastal ferry. Through the open doors, dock lamps laid narrow stripes across the tide. He pushed a pallet of canned sardines toward the storage racks and entered its weight in the ledger. Outside, a small cargo ship moved between the buoys, leaving waves that tapped the seawall. At midnight, he ate bread beside a window overlooking the fishing boats and their folded nets. A coworker brought another manifest from the pier, and Malik matched its numbers to boxes of marine fittings. By three, the tide had dropped below a band of mussels on the harbor wall. He swept salt from the warehouse threshold, returned the broom, and recorded the final shipment as the first ferry crossed the bay.

At midnight, Malik worked beneath the strip lights of a warehouse, stacking cartons beside a loading bay. His scanner logged every pallet he moved, including the extra twelve his supervisor had left beside the shutter. By three, sweat had soaked his collar and cardboard dust coated his tongue. Then the supervisor handed him a warning for missing quota. Malik pointed to the scanner totals. The supervisor cleared the screen with one thumb. “Those went under my number.” Across the desk lay a bonus form bearing the supervisor’s signature. Malik read it twice. Heat climbed from his chest into his face; his jaw locked so tightly that a tooth throbbed. He had skipped both breaks for those pallets. Now his work had bought someone else a reward and him a penalty. He pushed the warning back, slowly, before his hands could crumple it. “Print the original logs.” When the supervisor reached for the paper, Malik planted his palm over it.

Malik began his night shift beneath the warehouse’s red ceiling lamps, beside a stack of crimson plastic pallets. He hung his burgundy jacket on a hook and took a clipboard covered in red vinyl. The first sheet listed cartons of scarlet ribbon, red ceramic bowls, and folded maroon tablecloths. He counted each carton, marked the quantities with a red pencil, and moved the boxes onto a brick-red trolley. Along the central aisle, red tape divided the concrete floor into numbered storage bays. Malik placed the ribbon beneath a vermilion shelf label and arranged the bowls behind a red mesh barrier. At midnight, he ate from a red lunch container beside the vending machine’s cherry-colored panel. He then returned to the loading area, where another worker passed him a roll of dark red packing film. Before the shift ended, Malik wrapped the remaining pallets and filed his sheet in a crimson binder.

At two in the morning, Malik scanned cartons beneath the warehouse lights while rain struck the loading bay roof. He had almost finished his aisle when a metallic crack came from the shelving above him. A bolt bounced beside his boot. He looked up and saw the highest pallet slide forward, its plastic wrapping stretched white around a load of machine parts. He stepped backward into his cart. The rack tilted another inch, and the crossbar behind him bent across the narrow exit. His scanner slipped from his fingers. He crouched beneath the lowest shelf, drawing his knees against his chest as boxes burst across the concrete. The shelf above his head began to buckle. He pressed both palms against the floor, but his hands kept skidding in his own sweat. Somewhere beyond the aisle, footsteps approached. He tried to call out. Only a thin breath escaped before another bolt struck the floor.

At two in the morning, Agnes stood beside a conveyor belt beneath the warehouse’s fluorescent lights. The last truck waited outside, but six cartons were missing from a hospital shipment. She checked the loading bays, then followed a trail of torn blue wrapping to a pallet behind the empty crates. There they were, stacked beneath the wrong routing label. Agnes dragged over a trolley and loaded it so quickly that her sleeves slipped past her elbows. The driver scanned the final carton with three minutes to spare. Every box showed green on the shipment screen. Agnes pressed both hands against her mouth, then laughed into her palms. Her chest seemed too small for the breath filling it. She had caught it; the boxes would arrive before morning. As the truck pulled away, she bounced twice on her toes and swept the loading-bay floor in wide, dancing arcs.

Agnes began her night shift at the warehouse by counting cartons beneath the overhead lights. The first rack held 28 cartons, and the second held 34; she wrote 28 + 34 = 62 on her clipboard. After 17 cartons moved to the loading bay, she recorded 62 − 17 = 45 remaining. Each carton contained 12 packets, so she calculated 45 × 12 = 540 packets. She divided that inventory among 9 marked sections: 540 ÷ 9 = 60 packets per section. A forklift passed through the adjoining aisle while she checked the shelf labels. At the packing bench, she counted 8 bundles of 25 sleeves and entered 8 × 25 = 200. She used 36 sleeves, leaving 200 − 36 = 164. Outside, truck lights crossed the high windows. Agnes stacked the unused sleeves, replaced the pencil beside the ledger, and walked to the next rack with her clipboard.

Agnes entered the warehouse through the side door and hung her coat on a hook beside the lockers. She collected a scanner from its charging station, checked the label on a cart, and pushed it toward the shelving. Overhead lights shone across the concrete floor. She scanned each carton before placing it on the cart, keeping the labels facing outward. At the loading area, another worker took the cart and left an empty one beside her. Agnes wiped dust from the scanner screen with a cloth. Later, she sat at a table in the break room, ate a sandwich, and rinsed her cup beneath the tap. She returned to the aisles and gathered loose packing paper into a bin. A truck stood outside the loading doors while workers moved pallets inside. Near the end of her shift, Agnes returned the scanner, collected her coat, and walked out through the side door.

At two in the morning, Dmitri stood beneath the warehouse strip lights beside a row of shrink-wrapped pallets. He had spent six hours unloading trucks while the supervisor’s nephew sat in the office watching videos. When the last trailer arrived, Dmitri asked for his scheduled break. The supervisor blocked the doorway and pointed at the clock. “Finish first.” Through the office window, Dmitri saw the nephew signing out, his untouched gloves tucked into his belt. Then the supervisor marked Dmitri’s sheet: thirty minutes deducted for a break he had never taken. Heat climbed his neck. He pressed his tongue against his teeth until his jaw throbbed. Six hours, and they were taking more. He gripped the pallet jack so tightly that the handle trembled, then set it down with a crack that stopped conversation across the loading bay. He pulled the timesheet from beneath the supervisor’s hand and circled the deduction hard enough to tear the paper.

At two in the morning, Agnes stood beside the warehouse conveyor beneath strips of fluorescent light. She had spent six hours clearing a backlog while the supervisor sat behind his office window. When the final pallet rolled away, he handed her a warning slip for falling below quota. His own login number appeared beside forty-seven cartons she had scanned. Agnes pointed to the screen. He turned it off. “Sign it before you leave.” Heat climbed from her collar to her scalp. She pressed her thumb against the pen until the clip snapped, then laid both pieces on his desk. He had taken her work, and now he expected her signature beneath the lie. Her jaw locked so tightly that her molars ached. She pictured sweeping his tidy stacks onto the concrete. Instead, she photographed the warning, the scanner history, and his login card. Then she pulled the unsigned slip back from his reaching hand.

Agnes began her night shift at the warehouse beside the harbor, where seawater rose against the stone quay. She checked a shipment of rope while fishing boats moved between the outer buoys and the docks. Beyond the loading doors, small waves folded beneath a row of moored coastal freighters. She entered crate numbers in a ledger, matching each entry to labels stamped with ports along the northern coastline. At midnight, the tide reached the third iron rung of the quay ladder, and she rolled a pallet of canned sardines toward storage. Another worker brought shipping forms from a vessel carrying salt from an island refinery. Agnes fastened the forms to a clipboard as a seal surfaced near the harbor steps. During her break, she ate bread beside a window overlooking the channel and its navigation lights. Before dawn, she counted the remaining crates while the ebb exposed bands of seaweed on the quay.

At two in the morning, Dmitri stood beneath the warehouse strip lights beside a conveyor stacked with cartons. The last truck waited outside, but a jammed sorting gate had backed orders halfway across the floor. He switched off the belt, knelt, and found a torn packing strap wound around the lower hinge. His gloves slipped twice before he worked it loose. When he restarted the line, the gate snapped cleanly into place. Cartons rolled toward their proper loading bays, one after another, without a single wrong turn. The supervisor checked the departure screen and raised both thumbs. They would make the deadline; everyone would get home on time. Dmitri's grin stretched until his cheeks ached. He bounced once on his toes, then caught a passing carton with a flourish. All those stalled boxes, moving because of his hands. He carried that thought through the remaining hour like a song he couldn't stop humming.

At midnight, Agnes worked beneath the warehouse strip lights, scanning cartons beside the loading bays. Her phone rested on a stack of packing slips, playing the voicemail her mother had left before going into hospital six months earlier. “Bring my blue slippers.” Agnes listened to it every break; there were no other recordings. When a pallet struck the table, the phone slid beneath a reversing forklift. She raised one hand, too late. The driver stopped and helped her collect the pieces, setting them in a shallow cardboard tray. Agnes pressed the broken power button until its jagged edge marked her thumb. She tried to recall exactly how her mother had pronounced slippers, but the voice in her head had already become her own. Behind her, cartons continued down the conveyor. She folded a packing slip over the shattered screen and sat on the concrete, holding the tray level in both hands.

Dmitri entered the warehouse through the side door and hung his coat beside the lockers. He checked the shift sheet, collected a scanner, and walked to the loading area. Overhead lamps lit the concrete floor and the rows of wrapped pallets. He scanned the labels on a cart, then pushed it toward the shelving along the far wall. At each marked location, he transferred a carton and checked its label against the screen. A coworker passed with an empty pallet jack. Dmitri moved the cart aside until the aisle was clear, then continued along the row. During his break, he sat at a table and ate a sandwich from a paper bag. Afterward, he put the bag in a bin and returned to the floor. He replaced a roll of packing tape, stacked some folding crates, and entered the completed tasks in the shift log before collecting his coat.

At midnight, Dmitri drove a pallet jack between the warehouse loading bays and the rows of shrink-wrapped crates. Near three, his supervisor handed him a cardboard box from the locker room. They needed the locker for a new hire; his father’s things had stayed there long enough. Dmitri set the box beside the time clock. Inside lay a thermos, a spare pair of socks, and the reading glasses he had searched for after the funeral. One lens still bore a thumbprint. He lifted the thermos and unscrewed its lid. The faint smell of coffee remained beneath the metal smell, and his knees bent until he was sitting on an empty pallet. For thirty years, his father had brought that flask to work. Dmitri pressed the lid against his mouth. When the loading bell rang, he tried to stand, but stayed seated, holding the box steady while his chest hitched and the glasses blurred.

At two in the morning, Agnes scanned cartons beneath the warehouse’s fluorescent lights. She had almost finished her aisle when a metallic crack sounded overhead.
