A bolt struck the concrete beside her shoe. She looked up. The highest shelf leaned outward, its shrink-wrapped pallets nudging the beam below. Agnes stepped back, but her heel caught beneath a broken pallet slat. She pulled once, hard. Her shoe stayed wedged. Above her, metal scraped metal with a long, thinning note. There was nowhere to duck; stacked refrigerators blocked both sides of the aisle. Her mouth dried so completely that her call emerged as a breath. She pictured the morning crew finding her scanner blinking beneath the wreckage. With shaking fingers, she clawed at her shoelaces, unable to locate the knot. Another bolt dropped. She tore her foot free of the shoe and scrambled backward as the first carton tipped into empty air.

Agnes began her night shift at the warehouse by hanging her burgundy coat beside a row of red lockers. She collected a crimson clipboard and followed the maroon floor stripe toward the packing tables. Beneath red pendant lamps, cartons of scarlet ribbon stood in stacks marked with white numbers. She counted each stack, entered the totals on a pink inventory sheet, and moved three cartons onto a red trolley. At midnight, a worker in a brick-red apron brought another pallet to her station. Agnes compared its labels with the entries in her burgundy ledger, then wrapped the boxes in transparent film printed with ruby dots. During her break, she drank water from a red cup beside the loading bay’s closed russet doors. She returned the cup to its shelf and resumed sorting crimson envelopes by size. Near dawn, she parked the trolley beneath a red shelf and hung the clipboard on its hook.

At two in the morning, Dmitri worked beneath the fluorescent lights of a warehouse lined with steel racks and shrink-wrapped pallets. He was scanning a carton when a metallic crack snapped through the aisle. Above him, a loaded beam sagged. Dust sifted onto his scanner, and the nearest upright twisted with a slow, grinding squeal. He stepped backward, but a parked forklift blocked the gap behind him. His pulse hammered against his collar. Three levels of stacked appliances leaned overhead; he pictured the narrow space beneath them disappearing. The scanner slipped from his wet fingers. He crouched and tried to squeeze beneath the forklift’s raised carriage, catching his jacket on a lever. Another bolt struck the concrete beside his shoe. He pulled until the fabric tore, crawled clear, and pressed himself behind a concrete pillar. When the racks collapsed, he covered his head, his mouth open around a breath that would not come.

Dmitri began his night shift at the harbor warehouse while the tide covered the lowest marks on the quay. Through the open loading doors, seawater reflected the lamps along a row of moored fishing boats. He checked a manifest for twelve crates of rope, then stacked them beside pallets of sea salt. A driver brought another load from the coastal road, and Dmitri recorded its weight beneath the warehouse clock. Between deliveries, he swept sand and fragments of dried seaweed from the floor into a metal pan. Outside, small waves passed beneath the pier, where mussels lined the wooden supports. He ate his bread beside a window overlooking the channel and a cargo ship moving toward the sea. At four, he counted insulated boxes intended for the morning fish market. When the tide began to fall, Dmitri closed the ledger and placed it on the desk facing the harbor.

Dmitri began his night shift beside a red loading door, where a burgundy clipboard hung from a hook. He checked the pallet numbers beneath red ceiling lamps and entered each sequence on a handheld terminal with a crimson case. Along the first aisle, scarlet cartons contained folded tablecloths, red plastic bowls, and rolls of brick-colored fabric. He moved three pallets onto marked squares of red tape, then returned the pallet jack to its maroon charging station. At midnight, he ate bread from a red lunchbox while the warehouse clock advanced above a row of vermilion lockers. Another worker passed him a sheet printed with red column headings, and Dmitri sorted it into a burgundy folder. Before dawn, he counted spools of ruby thread and stacked their red trays on a cart. His shift ended when he placed the crimson terminal in its dock and walked through the red loading door.

Dmitri began his night shift at the warehouse beside a rack of numbered bins. He counted 24 cartons on one pallet and 18 on another; 24 plus 18 equaled 42, which he entered on the inventory sheet. From those 42 cartons, he moved 7 to the loading area; 42 minus 7 left 35 beneath the rack. Each remaining carton held 6 packages, so he calculated 35 multiplied by 6 as 210 packages. He divided the 210 packages among 5 storage sections on his worksheet; 210 divided by 5 equaled 42 per section. Above him, fluorescent tubes lit the concrete aisles. A forklift passed the doorway while he measured a shelf and recorded its width. Later, he counted 12 empty containers, stacked them in 3 columns of 4, and checked the labels against the register. At the end of the shift, Dmitri placed the sheet in a tray and returned his pencil to its holder.

Chloe entered the museum through a glass doorway and placed her umbrella in the stand beside the entrance. She took a floor plan from the counter, then walked into a gallery of household objects. Clay bowls stood inside a display case, with labels listing their materials and places of origin. She read the labels and moved along the case to a row of metal spoons. In the next room, woven cloth hung behind glass. Chloe paused beside a wall panel, read its description of the weaving process, and continued toward the staircase. Upstairs, she passed framed architectural drawings and a model of a public building. A visitor stood near the model while a staff member adjusted a brochure rack. Chloe returned to the ground floor, put the floor plan in her bag, and collected her umbrella. She left through the same doorway and walked toward the bus stop.

Chloe entered the museum beside the harbor, where seawater reached the lower steps at high tide. Inside, a glass case held shells arranged by coastline, with small maps showing the waters where each species lived. She followed a corridor lined with paintings of cargo ships crossing the ocean beneath bands of cloud. In the next gallery, a model fishing boat rested above a diagram of currents along the continental shelf. Chloe read the labels beside preserved seahorses, coral branches, and a section of whale bone. Through an open window, waves moved against the harbor wall while a ferry passed between two buoys. She stopped at a table displaying maritime charts and traced a printed shipping route with one finger. Before leaving, she returned the museum leaflet to a stand beneath a photograph of the coast. Outside, she walked along the quay as the tide covered another row of stones.

Chloe entered the museum at 10:00 and took a folded floor plan from the stand. The first gallery held 12 clay bowls in one cabinet and 8 in another; she calculated 12 + 8 = 20 and recorded the total beside the gallery number. Of 30 spaces on a display rack, 7 were empty, so she wrote 30 − 7 = 23 occupied spaces. In the next room, 6 shelves each supported 4 stone fragments. Chloe multiplied 6 × 4 = 24, then checked the arrangement against the printed inventory. A wall panel listed 36 tiles divided equally among 9 excavated rooms; she worked out 36 ÷ 9 = 4 tiles per room. She continued along the marked route, copied two dates from a bronze vessel’s label, and measured a bench in paces. At 11:15, she returned the pencil to its holder and walked through the exit.

Chloe stood beneath the museum’s glass dome, beside a table covered with replicas of ancient pottery fragments. A sign invited visitors to reconstruct a bowl, but the pieces had defeated everyone that morning. She set down her coat and studied the painted swallows scattered across the shards. Twice, a curved edge slipped from its match. Then she noticed that one bird’s wing continued beneath another bird’s tail. Her hands moved faster. Piece after piece settled into place until only a small triangle remained. She fitted it beneath the rim, and the bowl stood complete. The attendant rang a little brass bell and turned the display card to reveal a photograph of the original. Every swallow matched. Chloe bounced on her toes, laughing so hard she had to press both hands over her mouth. She circled the table once more. She had brought the birds together, and now they seemed to fly.

Chloe stood beneath the glass dome of the museum’s fossil gallery, beside a staircase leading to the mineral collection. She had stopped to read a label when a sharp crack interrupted the recorded birdsong. A white line spread across the dome above her. At first she mistook it for a reflection, but then a glass splinter struck the display case beside her hand. The guard waved everyone toward the staircase. Chloe turned with the others, only to see a security shutter descending across the entrance. Her pulse hammered against her collar. She ran, shoes slipping on the polished floor, while more cracks snapped overhead. The shutter was already below her waist. She dropped to her knees and crawled beneath it, catching her coat on the metal edge. For one breath she could not move. She tore herself loose as the shutter struck the floor behind her, and the gallery filled with the sound of falling glass.

Kenji entered the museum through the side doors and wiped his shoes on the mat. He placed his umbrella in a stand, took a floor guide from the counter, and walked toward the pottery gallery. Glass cases held bowls, jars, and fragments from household vessels. He read the labels beneath them, then moved to a display of tools arranged on linen. A visitor stood near the doorway with a folded coat over one arm. Kenji passed into the next room, where wooden cabinets contained maps and drawings. He leaned forward to examine the lettering on a street plan without touching the glass. After walking along the remaining cabinets, he sat on a bench and adjusted his shoelace. He returned the floor guide to the counter, collected his umbrella, and left through the same doors. Outside, he followed the pavement toward the bus stop.

Chloe stood beneath the museum’s glass roof beside a display of fishing nets and wooden boats. She had come to see the new harbor exhibition, carrying the admission money her mother had tucked into a birthday card before her final hospital stay. In the last room, a motion sensor started a recording. Her mother’s voice filled the space, describing how she had mended sails as a girl. Chloe stopped with one foot lifted. Nobody had told her the museum had kept this interview. On the screen, her mother brushed hair from her forehead with two fingers, a gesture Chloe had almost forgotten. She pressed her knuckles against her mouth. When the recording ended, she stepped away, then back, making it begin again. Other visitors passed behind her. She watched until her legs trembled, waiting each time for the small intake of breath before the first word, unable to bear the silence that followed the last.

Chloe stood beneath the museum’s glass dome beside a display of quilts and handwritten household records. She had donated her grandmother’s quilt six months earlier, along with letters documenting every stitched square. Now the label credited a wealthy trustee with both the gift and the family history. Chloe checked the accession number against the receipt in her bag. It matched. At the information desk, she laid out the papers, but the attendant pushed them back without reading them. “The labels are approved,” he said. Behind him, a supervisor waved her aside to welcome a group carrying champagne flutes. Heat climbed Chloe’s neck. Her jaw tightened until her teeth ached. They had accepted the quilt from her hands, then rubbed those hands out of its history. She planted her receipt on the counter again, flattening its corners with trembling fingers. She would not move aside. Let their guests watch them try to erase her twice.

Chloe entered the museum through a vermilion doorway and placed her red umbrella in a cylindrical stand. Beneath a crimson ceiling, she collected a floor plan printed with burgundy borders. The first gallery contained scarlet ceramic bowls arranged on shelves covered in red linen. She walked past a brick-red cabinet displaying copper buttons, ruby glass beads, and squares of carmine velvet. Red light from a tinted window crossed the tiled floor beside her shoes. In the next room, Chloe read a label describing the pigments used in an old tapestry of red leaves and rust-colored branches. She stopped at a table where visitors could compare samples of madder-dyed wool against maroon cards. An unnamed attendant replaced a red pencil beside the register. Chloe marked the final gallery on her map, returned through the vermilion doorway, and removed her umbrella from the stand. Outside, she followed the red paving stones toward the street.

Kenji entered the museum at ten and took a floor plan from the counter. The first gallery contained 12 glass cases, and the adjoining room contained 8; he calculated 12 + 8 = 20 cases across both rooms. He counted 35 ceramic bowls on a shelf and noted that 9 had lids, leaving 35 − 9 = 26 without lids. Beside a wall of tiles, he worked out that 6 rows multiplied by 7 columns made 42 tiles. A display divided 48 stone beads equally among 4 trays, so he calculated 48 ÷ 4 = 12 beads per tray. He copied the four calculations into his notebook beneath the gallery numbers. Upstairs, he measured his route on the map: 3 sections of 15 meters totaled 45 meters. He followed that route past the textile cases, returned the floor plan to the counter, and left through the side entrance.

Kenji stood beneath the glass dome of a maritime museum, beside a display of brass diving helmets. He had almost finished reading a placard when a metallic crack sounded overhead. A thin white line crossed the dome, branching above the crowded gallery. Then a bolt struck the floor near his shoe. He looked up and saw an entire pane sagging in its frame. His mouth dried. Beyond the display cases, visitors continued studying ship models, unaware of the shifting glass. “Move away from the center,” he said, but his voice barely carried. Another crack snapped through the hall. Kenji seized the nearest visitor’s sleeve and pulled her beneath a stone arch, his knees knocking against the wall. The dome would fall; he pictured its edges entering his neck, his hands, the backs of people still walking below. He pressed himself against the stone as fragments began ticking across the tiles, and waited for the weight above them to come down.

Kenji stood beneath the museum’s glass ceiling, beside a table covered with pottery fragments and a photograph of an ancient bowl. A sign invited visitors to assemble a replica, but the pieces slipped apart whenever he tried to fit the painted branches together. He rolled up his sleeves. Around him, shoes clicked across the marble floor. Then he noticed a tiny blue petal on the underside of one fragment. He turned it over, shifted two others, and suddenly the whole pattern made sense. The final piece settled into place with a soft click. A lamp inside the table switched on, sending the bowl’s flowering silhouette across the ceiling. Kenji tipped his head back. His laugh escaped so loudly that a nearby visitor looked up and laughed too. He bounced onto his toes, grinning until his cheeks ached. He had made those scattered branches bloom.

Mira entered the museum through the side entrance and placed her umbrella in the stand beside the door. At the desk, she collected a paper map and folded it along its existing creases. She walked into a gallery containing clay vessels, stone tools, and fragments of patterned cloth. Each case had a label mounted beneath the glass. Mira read several labels, then moved to a bench to adjust the strap of her bag. A group of visitors passed through the doorway behind her. In the next room, she examined a wooden cabinet with shallow drawers and brass handles. She followed the corridor to a display of architectural drawings, where she compared a building sketch with a photograph beside it. Before leaving, she returned the map to a tray at the desk, collected her umbrella, and stepped onto the pavement outside.

Kenji entered the museum through a vermilion doorway and placed his red umbrella in a cylindrical stand. At the ticket desk, he received a crimson paper pass printed with the floor plan. He followed a burgundy carpet into a gallery where red glass bowls stood on square plinths. Ruby light from a stained glass window crossed the tiles beneath his shoes. He read a label beside a scarlet lacquer cabinet, then moved toward a case of copper plates mounted on red velvet. In the next room, brick-red fabric panels divided rows of ceramic vessels glazed in rust and cherry shades. Kenji stopped at each numbered display and checked the corresponding entry in his red booklet. A museum attendant in a maroon jacket pointed toward the final gallery. There, he examined a red sandstone column before returning along the burgundy carpet, collecting his umbrella, and leaving through the vermilion doorway.

Kenji stood beneath the museum’s glass dome beside a case of bronze vessels. He had saved for weeks to see the newly opened gallery, and his ticket included admission. At its entrance, an attendant stretched an arm across the doorway and pointed to a handwritten surcharge. While Kenji searched his wallet, two visitors walked past without paying. The attendant nodded them through, then tapped the sign again for him.

“They’re different,” the attendant said.

Heat climbed Kenji’s neck. He pressed his ticket flat against the counter, hard enough to whiten his fingertips. Different how? His money had bought the same printed promise. Behind the attendant, the gallery remained open, bright, available to everyone except him. His jaw locked; each breath scraped through his nose. He wanted to sweep the neat stack of brochures onto the floor. Instead, he demanded a supervisor, keeping his palm planted while the paper crumpled beneath it.

Mira entered the museum beside the harbor, where seawater reached the lowest steps at high tide. In the first gallery, she examined a chart of the coastline and traced the printed route between two ports with one finger. A glass case held shells, coral fragments, and a brass instrument once used aboard a coastal survey ship. She read the labels, then moved to a model showing how waves carried sand along a beach. Beyond the windows, fishing boats crossed the harbor between rows of floating buoys. Upstairs, she stopped beside a whale skeleton suspended above cabinets of preserved marine specimens. A museum worker adjusted a label beneath a collection of sea urchins while Mira consulted the floor plan. She finished her visit in a room of navigation maps and tide tables. Outside, she followed the seawall toward the ferry landing, carrying a folded leaflet about the coastal collections.

Kenji entered the maritime museum beside the harbor, where seawater rose against the stone quay. He placed his ticket beneath a scanner and followed a floor mosaic of the coastline toward the first gallery. Behind glass, shells stood in rows beside labels listing the depths and tides of their habitats. A model cargo ship occupied the next case, its painted hull level with a strip of blue representing the sea. Kenji walked around it, then examined a chart showing channels between offshore islands. Through the gallery windows, fishing boats crossed the harbor while small waves reached the museum steps. Upstairs, he viewed preserved seaweed, whale vertebrae, and photographs of coastal tide pools. He read a panel describing how seawater moved through an estuary during each tidal cycle. Before leaving, he returned a laminated harbor map to its rack and recorded the museum’s coastal address in his notebook.

Mira walked through the museum’s maritime gallery beneath a ceiling hung with wooden boats. She carried a cassette in her coat pocket, the last recording of her father describing his years at sea. He had donated his compass to the museum, and she had come to hear his voice at the listening station beside it. But the alcove held a bright touchscreen now. A label described the compass as an anonymous gift. She tapped through every menu, then asked an attendant about the old recordings. They had been discarded during renovation. Mira pressed the cassette’s ridged edge into her palm. At home, its tape had snapped; she had counted on the museum’s copy. She sat before the glass case and opened her mouth, trying to recall how he had pronounced the name of his first ship. Nothing came. Her throat worked against each breath. When visitors approached, she lowered her head over the cassette and let them pass.

Mira walked between glass display cases in the museum’s basement gallery, beneath a row of narrow windows. She was studying a bronze key when the lights went out. A heavy door slammed somewhere behind her, followed by a sharp electrical crack. Orange light flickered through the ventilation grille. Then smoke began spilling between its slats.

She hurried back to the stairs, one hand sliding along the wall. The door at the top would not open. She pushed harder, then threw her shoulder against it. Nothing moved.

“Is anyone there?”

Her voice sounded small against the metal. Heat gathered above her head. She crouched, coughing, and fumbled for her phone with fingers that kept missing the pocket. No signal. The windows were too high, too narrow. Had anyone seen her come downstairs?

Footsteps crossed the floor overhead. Mira struck the door with both fists, counting each retreating step until she could no longer hear them.

Mira entered the museum at ten and collected a floor plan. The first gallery contained 18 ceramic bowls in one cabinet and 24 in another; she calculated 18 + 24 = 42 and wrote the total beside the gallery number. Of 35 numbered display spaces, 8 stood empty, so she recorded 35 - 8 = 27 occupied spaces. Along the opposite wall, 6 shelves each held 7 stone fragments. She multiplied 6 × 7 = 42, then checked the arrangement shelf by shelf. Upstairs, 48 prints were distributed equally among 4 rooms. Mira divided 48 ÷ 4 = 12 before entering the first room. She measured the route on her map: three sections of 20 meters gave 3 × 20 = 60 meters. At a bench, she counted 16 pages in the guide and subtracted the 9 she had turned, leaving 16 - 9 = 7. She read those pages, returned the floor plan, and left through the courtyard.

Kenji walked through the textile gallery beneath a row of narrow skylights. He had come to see the loom his mother had donated before her death, carrying the claim ticket she had kept in her sewing box. Beside the loom stood a listening station. He pressed its button, expecting a curator’s explanation. His mother’s voice emerged instead, counting threads, then humming the tune she used to sing while mending his school trousers. His hand stayed against the button. He had deleted her last voicemail to make room on his phone; for three years, he had been unable to remember exactly how she sounded. Now she paused in the recording and cleared her throat, an ordinary little scrape that bent him forward. He sat on the floor beside the bench. When the recording ended, he pressed the button again, holding the claim ticket until its folded edges cut into his palm.

Mira stood beneath the museum’s glass dome with a special exhibition ticket folded inside her guidebook. At the gallery entrance, an attendant scanned it, then blocked the doorway with his arm. The museum had oversold admission, he explained; she would have to leave. Behind him, several visitors bought fresh tickets from another attendant and walked straight through. Mira showed him her receipt, purchased weeks earlier, and the train fare she had paid to get there. He glanced past her and waved another couple inside. “Those are premium guests.” Heat climbed her neck. Her fingers tightened around the guidebook until its glossy cover buckled. So her money counted when they took it, but her place disappeared when someone paid more. She planted both feet before the scanner. When he reached for her ticket, she pulled it against her chest. “Get your supervisor.” Each word scraped through her clenched teeth. This time, he would have to look at her.

Mira stood beneath the museum’s glass dome, beside a table covered with curved pottery fragments. A sign invited visitors to reconstruct a replica bowl before looking at the original. She rolled up her sleeves and began sorting edges from centers. Twice, the rim collapsed onto the padded mat. She tried again, turning one stubborn piece until its painted stem joined a flower. After that, the pattern unfolded under her hands. When she fitted the final fragment, the attendant opened a small curtain behind the table. There stood the ancient bowl, its blue flowers arranged exactly like hers. Mira’s breath caught. She bounced on her toes, then laughed so hard she had to press her fingers against her lips. Her hands had figured it out. She circled the table to admire every side, cheeks aching, and asked the attendant to take her photograph beside both bowls. For once, she wanted proof that she had been there.

Mira entered the museum through a vermilion doorway and placed her red umbrella in a cylindrical stand. At the counter, an attendant handed her a ticket printed on rose paper beside a stack of crimson maps. She followed a burgundy runner into a gallery containing red clay vessels, each arranged on a square plinth. The labels listed dates, regions, and materials in black type beneath narrow scarlet headings. Mira stopped before a cabinet of carnelian beads and read the inventory numbers along its red velvet base. In the next room, ruby glass panels filtered daylight across a table covered with faded madder cloth. She examined a woven sash whose red stripes alternated with small unbleached squares. Near the exit, a brick-colored bench stood below a lacquered screen depicting red cranes among reeds. Mira checked the map once more, returned it to the counter, and collected her umbrella beneath the vermilion arch.

Andrei entered the museum through the glass doors and placed his folded umbrella in the stand beside the entrance. He bought a ticket at the counter, took a printed floor plan, and walked into the first gallery. A row of clay vessels stood inside a long display case. He read the labels, then moved toward a cabinet containing metal tools and fragments of woven cloth. In the next room, benches faced a group of landscape paintings. Andrei sat on a bench while he checked the floor plan. Other visitors passed through the doorway and continued along the wall. He stood, adjusted the strap of his bag, and followed the corridor to an exhibit of household furniture. Before leaving, he stopped at the drinking fountain near the stairs. He returned the floor plan to a tray, collected his umbrella, and stepped onto the pavement outside.

Andrei entered the museum through a red wooden door and placed his umbrella beside a crimson bench. At the counter, an attendant handed him a ticket printed on scarlet paper. He followed a burgundy runner into a gallery where red glass panels tinted the afternoon light. The first case contained cinnabar bowls, a brick-red jug, and several beads arranged on rust-colored linen. Andrei read the labels and copied three dates into a notebook with a maroon cover. Beyond the case, vermilion tiles formed a rectangular border around a mosaic of red clay squares. He stopped beside a scarlet curtain while a group passed between two rosewood cabinets. In the next room, red lamps illuminated woven fabrics ranging from coral to deep carmine. Andrei checked the gallery number against his red-edged map, then returned along the burgundy runner. He collected his umbrella and left through the red door at four.

Andrei stood beneath the museum’s glass dome beside a display of bronze vessels. He had saved for the exhibition ticket and carried his grandfather’s sketchbook, hoping to compare its drawings with the originals. At the gallery entrance, a guard stopped him and demanded that he surrender the book. Andrei pointed to visitors carrying larger notebooks past the same desk. The guard glanced at his patched coat, then reached for the sketchbook without answering. A brittle page caught beneath the man’s thumb and tore across a drawing. Heat climbed Andrei’s neck. He snatched the book back, his fingers shaking against its leather cover. “You tore it.” The guard shrugged and pointed toward the exit. Behind him, another visitor opened a sketchpad before a bronze bowl. Andrei’s teeth pressed together until his jaw ached. He planted both feet beside the desk and demanded a supervisor, each word scraping out slowly while the torn page trembled in his hand.

Andrei stood beside a glass cabinet in the museum’s newly opened music gallery. Inside lay the brass cylinder he had donated six months earlier, discovered beneath loose boards in his grandfather’s attic. The conservators had warned him that its grooves might be too damaged to recover. Now a curator slipped on headphones, adjusted a dial, and nodded toward a bench. Andrei sat with his hands pressed between his knees. Static crackled from a speaker. Then a violin emerged, thin but steady, playing the tune his grandfather had hummed while making Sunday pancakes. Andrei sprang upright. He clapped both hands over his mouth, then laughed into his palms as the melody climbed. They had saved it. Every note was there. His cheeks ached from smiling. When the recording ended, he wiped his eyes with his sleeve and leaned toward the curator, almost bouncing on his toes. “Could we hear it again?”

Andrei entered the maritime museum beside the harbor, where seawater rose along the stone quay with the afternoon tide. He left his coat at the counter and followed a floor map shaped like the coastline. The first gallery contained fishing nets, oyster shells, and a wooden model of a coastal cargo ship. He read a label explaining how tides altered the routes between nearby islands. Beyond the glass doors, small waves passed beneath moored boats. In the next room, preserved seahorses stood in jars beside diagrams of eelgrass beds and sandy seabeds. Andrei compared the markings on two nautical charts, then examined a brass instrument used aboard sailing ships. A museum worker replaced a card beneath a display of sea urchins. He checked the time under a painting of an estuary and returned his guidebook to the shelf. Outside, he walked along the harbor wall while the tide covered another row of stones.

At seven fifteen, Ingrid stood beneath the bus shelter as rain threaded down the glass and headlights swept the road. When the bus arrived, she stepped aboard and pressed her pass against the reader. It flashed red. She showed the driver the renewal receipt on her phone, dated that morning, but he pointed toward the pavement. “Pay cash or get off.” She had no cash. Behind her, a man waved an unreadable pass and received a nod toward the seats. Ingrid stayed beside the reader. Heat climbed her neck; her jaw tightened until a tooth ached. Her wages had paid for that pass, and now this man could make her late with one flick of his hand. She wanted to wrench the reader from its bracket. Instead, she planted both feet and held up the receipt again, her hand shaking so hard that the screen rattled against its cracked case.

Andrei entered the museum at ten and took a printed floor plan from the counter. The first gallery held eight stone vessels along one wall and six along another; he added 8 + 6 = 14 and wrote the total beside the gallery number. In the next room, twenty display spaces included seven empty stands, so he calculated 20 - 7 = 13 occupied spaces. He walked past four cabinets containing nine ceramic tiles each and recorded 4 × 9 = 36 tiles. Upstairs, thirty bronze objects had been arranged equally across five shelves; he divided 30 ÷ 5 = 6 objects per shelf. Beside a scale model, he counted twelve columns on each of two sides and noted 12 × 2 = 24. He then compared his notes with the labels, folded the floor plan into quarters, and left through the courtyard entrance at eleven.

Andrei stood beneath the glass dome of the museum, between a marble staircase and a display of ancient coins. He had just leaned toward a silver piece when a sharp crack sounded overhead. A white line raced across the dome. Then another appeared, branching above the visitors like a river on a map. A guard waved everyone toward the staircase, but a metal security shutter dropped across its entrance. Andrei stopped so abruptly that someone struck his back. His mouth dried. Through the glass, he saw a maintenance platform tilt, its broken cable swinging loose. The platform slid another inch. He pictured the weight coming down, the shards passing through his raised hands. His knees bent without his permission. He crawled behind the stone base of a statue and pulled a stranger down beside him. Above them, bolts popped one after another. He pressed his forehead against the cold marble and waited for the next sound.

Ingrid left her apartment with a canvas bag over her shoulder and walked to the bus stop beside the pharmacy. The timetable stood behind a scratched plastic cover. She checked the route label, then took her transit card from an outer pocket. When the bus arrived, she stepped aboard, held the card against the reader, and moved down the aisle. She sat beside a window and placed the bag on her lap. Across from her, a passenger held a folded newspaper. Another stood near the doors with a hand around a pole. The bus passed a bakery, a parking garage, and a row of apartment buildings. At each stop, people stepped off or came aboard. Ingrid adjusted the strap of her bag and looked through the window at the storefronts. Near her workplace, she pressed the stop button. She left through the rear doors and walked toward the office entrance.

Ingrid boarded the morning bus beside the harbor, where seawater rose against stone steps beneath the quay. She scanned her pass and took a window seat facing the channel between two stretches of coastline. Beyond the glass, gulls stood on mooring posts, and fishing boats crossed the incoming tide. The bus followed the coastal road past a fish market whose open loading doors faced the docks. Ingrid placed her bag on her knees while rows of oyster cages passed offshore. At the next stop, passengers entered carrying lunch containers, with a ferry moving behind them across the bay. She checked the time as the bus rounded a curve above a beach patterned by retreating waves. A cargo ship remained visible beyond the breakwater when she pressed the stop button. Ingrid stepped onto the pavement near her workplace, and the bus continued along the seawall toward another harbor.

At seven each morning, Ingrid boarded the number twelve bus beneath the railway bridge and sat beside the rear window. For eleven years, her husband had occupied the aisle seat until his shift changed in March. Now she rested her lunch bag there and watched the bakery shutters rise. At the next stop, the driver handed her a blue wool glove. “Found this behind the heater.” She recognized the crooked seam she had stitched across its thumb last winter. For a moment she turned toward the aisle, already lifting it to show him. Then her hand stopped. His new shift had lasted nine days before the scaffolding fell. The bus pulled away while she pressed the glove flat against her knee, smoothing each empty finger. She tried to remember whether he had complained about losing it, but could summon only the hospital telephone ringing. When her stop came, she remained seated, holding the glove open with both hands.

At seven fifteen, Ingrid boarded the morning bus beneath the railway bridge and took a seat halfway down the aisle. She tucked her lunch under her knees and watched shopkeepers roll up their shutters. On the hill above the river, the driver pressed the brake pedal twice. The bus kept gathering speed. He pressed again, harder, and reached for a lever beside his seat.

“The brakes aren’t working.”

Ingrid’s fingers locked around the seat rail. Ahead, traffic stood motionless at the red light, with a tanker across both lanes. Her mouth dried so completely that she couldn’t swallow. She pictured the narrow gap beneath the tanker, then pushed the image away. There wasn’t room. There wasn’t time. As the driver swung toward a side street, she dropped below the window and covered her head. Her lunch slid away. She kept her eyes on a screw in the floor while the tires shrieked.

The morning bus carried Ingrid past shuttered shops and a bakery unloading trays onto the pavement. She stood near the rear doors, one hand around a pole, the other holding her phone. For three weeks, she had checked the same application page between stops. That morning, the spinning circle vanished and a new line appeared beneath her name: accepted, with full funding. She read it twice, then pressed her thumb against each word as if testing whether it would stay. Her knees bent unexpectedly; she caught the pole and laughed into her scarf. The passenger beside her shifted, making room on a seat. Ingrid sat, stood again, and sat once more. All those evenings studying after work had led somewhere. She could actually go. At the next stop, she helped lift a stroller aboard, grinning so broadly her cheeks ached. When the bus pulled away, she watched her reflection smiling back from every passing window.

Ingrid reached the bus stop at seven, carrying a red canvas bag beneath her burgundy coat. The timetable sat inside a crimson frame, beside an advertisement showing tomatoes in a scarlet bowl. She checked the route number as a bus with maroon side panels pulled alongside the curb. Inside, red fabric covered the seats, and ruby light from a bakery sign crossed the windows. Ingrid placed her bag on her knees and held a ticket printed with a thin red border. Across the aisle, a passenger folded a newspaper over a vermilion lunch container. The bus passed brick warehouses, red awnings, and a bicycle with cherry-colored wheel rims. At the next stop, two passengers boarded with matching russet shopping bags. Ingrid adjusted the red cuff beneath her coat sleeve and checked her watch. When the bus reached her stop, she stepped onto the pavement beside a red postbox.

Ingrid reached the bus stop at 7:12 and checked the posted schedule. The bus arrived at 7:18, so she subtracted 12 from 18 and recorded 6 minutes in her notebook. Inside, she counted 8 rows with 4 seats each; 8 multiplied by 4 equaled 32 seats. There were 19 passengers seated, leaving 32 minus 19, or 13 empty places. She took a seat beside the window and opened her route map. The first section covered 3 kilometers, and the second covered 5; 3 plus 5 equaled 8 kilometers. Over the next stretch, the bus traveled 6 kilometers in 12 minutes. She divided 6 by 12, obtaining 0.5 kilometers per minute. At a stop, 4 passengers boarded and 2 departed, bringing the passenger count to 22, including Ingrid. She wrote 20 plus 4 minus 2 equaled 22, closed the notebook, and watched the numbered stops pass until she reached her usual intersection.

Andrei stood beneath the museum’s glass roof beside a display of household objects recovered from the flooded valley. He had donated his mother’s sewing box years earlier, wrapped in a towel, without opening it. Now it sat beneath a light, its compartments arranged for strangers to inspect. Among the buttons and needles lay a folded paper newly uncovered by the curator. He bent toward the label. It was a list in his mother’s handwriting: trousers to shorten, curtains to finish, blue shirt for Andrei’s birthday. The date was three days before the river took her house. He pressed two fingers against the glass, directly above his name. His throat tightened until swallowing hurt. All these years, he had pictured her waiting for rescue; here she was planning his sleeves. He sat on the bench opposite the case and kept his coat on, unable to leave her work unfinished behind him.

At seven fifteen, Viktor boarded the morning bus beneath the railway bridge, his lunch tin tucked under one arm. He tapped his pass, and the reader blinked green. The driver waved him back. “Pay again.” Viktor pointed to the light and the fresh charge on his phone, but the driver covered the reader with one hand and ordered him off unless he paid cash. Behind him, shoes scraped and someone clicked their tongue. Then a man in a quilted coat climbed aboard, nodded at the driver, and walked past without paying. Heat climbed Viktor’s neck. His teeth pressed together until his jaw ached. Apparently the rules were only for people the driver could push around. He counted coins onto the tray, each one striking harder than the last. At the rear window, he gripped his lunch tin until its thin lid buckled, rehearsing every detail he would put in the complaint.

Viktor left his apartment after breakfast and pulled the door until the latch caught. He walked along the pavement, passing a bakery with trays stacked behind its window. At the bus stop, he stood beside the timetable and adjusted the strap of his shoulder bag. The bus arrived while a delivery van was turning into a side street. Viktor stepped aboard, held his pass against the reader, and took a seat near the middle. A passenger across the aisle had a folded newspaper resting on a canvas bag. Water marks covered part of the window beside him. At each stop, people moved along the aisle, and the doors opened toward the curb. Viktor checked the street signs as the bus continued past offices and shops. When his stop came, he pressed the button, collected his bag, and stepped onto the pavement.

Viktor reached the bus stop beside a red brick wall, carrying a burgundy canvas bag. The timetable sat beneath a crimson header, and a red advertisement covered one side of the shelter. He checked his watch as a maroon bus approached along the morning route. Inside, red vinyl seats lined the aisle beneath narrow strips of ruby light. Viktor placed his pass against the reader, then took a seat beside a scarlet curtain. Across from him, a passenger held a red folder over a pair of rust-colored trousers. The bus passed a bakery with red awnings, a shop displaying vermilion bowls, and several houses with terracotta roofs. At the next stop, two passengers boarded with matching crimson shopping bags. Viktor moved his burgundy bag onto his knees while the bus continued past a red sandstone building. At his usual stop, he stepped onto paving edged with reddish gravel and walked toward the office’s maroon doors.

At seven forty, Viktor rode the morning bus toward the river bridge, his lunch tin balanced on his knees. Rain striped the windows, and the aisle smelled of wet wool. He was checking the time when the driver pressed the brake twice, then stamped on it. The bus kept gathering speed. Ahead, red lights marked a queue of cars halfway across the bridge.

“Hold on,” the driver said.

Viktor shoved his lunch beneath the seat and gripped the metal rail. His palms slipped. The gap ahead shrank until he could see a child's hand against the rear window of the nearest car. He tried to swallow, but his throat would not move. There was nowhere wide enough for the bus to go. He braced his feet, bent over his knees, and waited for the impact, counting each second without meaning to, unable to get past three before starting again.

Viktor reached the bus stop at 7:18 and read the timetable beneath the route map. The next bus was listed for 7:24, so he subtracted 18 from 24 and obtained 6 minutes. He counted 8 windows along the side of a parked bus; with 2 seats beneath each window, 8 multiplied by 2 gave 16 seats. When his bus arrived, he boarded through the front door and sat beside the aisle. There were 12 passengers ahead of him and 7 behind him; 12 plus 7 equaled 19, or 20 with Viktor included. At the next stop, 4 passengers departed, and 20 minus 4 left 16. He divided the remaining 24 minutes of the ride among 6 stops, producing an average of 4 minutes per stop. Between intersections, he copied these calculations into a small notebook. At his usual stop, he closed the notebook, stood, and stepped onto the pavement.

Viktor reached the coastal bus stop at seven, while seawater covered the lower steps of the harbor quay. He stood beside a timetable whose glass reflected fishing boats and the pale stripe of the offshore horizon. When the bus arrived, he boarded with three other passengers carrying canvas bags marked with shellfish suppliers’ stamps. His usual route followed the seawall, passing tidal pools where small crabs moved between strands of seaweed. Through the window, he watched a ferry cross the bay behind rows of anchored sailboats. At the next stop, a worker loaded two empty fish crates into the luggage space beside the driver. Viktor checked his watch as the bus curved around an inlet bordered by oyster beds. He left the bus near the marine warehouse, crossed the pavement above the beach, and entered through a door facing the water.

The morning bus carried Viktor past shuttered shops and rows of parked cars beneath a pale October sky. He stood near the rear doors, holding a paper bag with two cheese rolls, one for himself and one for his mother at the hospital. She had asked for hers toasted, as though breakfast could settle the matter of another operation. His phone vibrated just before the river bridge. A nurse spoke while the bus rattled over a seam in the road. “She died a few minutes ago.” Viktor kept his thumb pressed against the warm bag. He asked whether he should still come, then listened without catching the answer. At the next stop, someone needed to pass him, but his knees would not bend. He moved only when a hand touched his sleeve. Sitting down, he carefully divided the rolls onto two napkins. Then he covered the second one, so it would not get cold.

At seven fifteen, Viktor stood beneath the bus shelter with a lunch tin and a folded bakery lease in his coat pocket. For six years, he had taken this bus to the warehouse, counting empty storefronts along the route. This morning, his phone stayed dark through four stops. He checked the signal, wiped the screen, and checked again. Just before the bridge, a message arrived from the landlord: the shop was his, and he could collect the keys that afternoon. Viktor read it twice. Then he pressed his fist against his mouth, but a laugh escaped between his fingers. His shoulders bounced. Outside, the river flashed between the bridge rails, and he could already picture trays of rolls cooling in his own window. He nearly missed his stop. On the pavement, he spun once with his lunch tin swinging, then hurried toward the warehouse, rehearsing how he would give notice.

Greta left her apartment after putting her lunch container into her bag. At the bus stop, she stood beside the timetable and watched a delivery van pass the bakery. A person near the shelter held a folded newspaper. When the bus arrived, Greta stepped aboard, tapped her travel card against the reader, and walked to an empty seat halfway down the aisle. She placed her bag on her lap. The windows carried thin streaks from an earlier shower, and the pavement outside was still wet. At the next stop, several passengers got on while another stepped off carrying a cloth shopping bag. Greta moved her shoes beneath the seat as someone passed. The bus continued along the main road, stopping beside a pharmacy and then a school fence. When her stop came, she pressed the button, stood, and left through the middle doors. She followed the pavement toward her office building.

Greta boarded the morning bus beneath a railway bridge, carrying her lunch and a folded newspaper. She took her usual seat near the front while rain striped the windows. At the next hill, the driver pressed the brake pedal, then stamped on it twice. The bus kept gathering speed. He pulled a lever beside his seat; nothing changed. Greta lowered her newspaper. Ahead, traffic stood motionless at a red light, the gap shrinking with every sweep of the wipers. Her fingers locked around the seat rail. She tried to swallow, but her throat would not work. There was nowhere to step, nothing to hold that could stop her body from flying forward. “Hold on,” the driver said. Greta ducked behind the seat, knees drawn tight, and heard a horn sustain one long note. The bus swerved onto the pavement. As branches struck the glass, she covered her head and waited for the impact.

At seven fifteen, Greta stood beneath the bus shelter while rain tapped the timetable and traffic crawled toward the station. She had arrived before everyone else, with her lunch tucked under one arm and exact change in her fist. When the bus stopped, a man stepped around her and planted himself in the doorway. The driver waved him aboard, then held up a hand against Greta.

“Full. Next one.”

Through the glass, she counted three empty seats. The man settled into one and put his bag on another. She pointed, but the driver closed the doors against her raised fingers. Heat climbed her neck. Her coins bit into her palm as the bus pulled away, spraying gutter water across her trousers. Another late arrival meant another warning at work; the driver had handed her that consequence without even looking at her. She kicked the shelter’s metal post hard enough to send a clang down the pavement.

At seven fifteen, Greta stood beneath the bus shelter while rain threaded the street and headlights crossed the puddles. She boarded with her lunch tucked under one arm and found a seat above the rear wheel. For three weeks, every morning commute had included the same ritual: opening her email, refreshing it, then putting the phone away.

This time, a new message appeared.

She read the first sentence twice. She had passed the licensing exam. Beneath it, the clinic confirmed her start date.

Greta pressed her knuckles against her mouth. A laugh slipped through anyway, and the passenger beside her glanced over. She turned the screen toward him as though he had been studying alongside her all winter.

“I passed,” she said.

He nodded, grinning. Greta's feet bounced against the floor. Outside, the bus crawled past the bakery, the laundromat, the shuttered shops. She sat taller, reading her new job title aloud under her breath.

Greta boarded the morning bus beside the harbor, where seawater reached the lower rungs of a quay ladder. She tapped her pass and took a window seat facing the channel and its anchored fishing boats. The bus followed the coastline, passing racks of oyster baskets and a warehouse stacked with coils of marine rope. Beyond the glass, small waves folded onto a narrow beach beneath the road. Greta placed her lunch container on her knees while a ferry crossed between two buoys. At the next stop, passengers entered carrying work bags, and gulls walked along the seawall behind them. The tide covered most of the rocks around the pier, leaving several bands of seaweed above the water. She checked the time as the bus passed a row of moored sailboats. When it reached the waterfront offices, Greta stepped onto the pavement and continued beside the harbor toward her building.

Greta reached the bus stop at seven, wearing a brick-red coat and carrying a burgundy canvas bag. Beneath the red shelter roof, she checked the timetable through a sheet of scratched plastic. A crimson bus arrived beside the curb, its windows reflecting the red lettering above a grocery shop. She tapped her scarlet travel card against the reader and walked along the aisle between rows of maroon seats. A passenger in a rust-red jacket moved a folded newspaper from the adjacent cushion. Greta sat with her bag across her knees while red light from a bakery sign crossed the window. At the next stop, two people boarded with matching vermilion shopping sacks. She took a red-covered notebook from her bag and copied three numbers from a receipt. When the bus reached her stop, she closed the notebook, passed the red handrail, and stepped onto the pavement beside a row of red rental bicycles.

Greta reached the bus stop at seven fifteen and stood beside the timetable. While the bus approached, she counted 8 rows of windows and calculated that 8 multiplied by 4 seats made 32 seats. Inside, she counted 19 passengers seated, then subtracted 19 from 32 to get 13 unoccupied seats. She took one beside the aisle and placed her bag beneath it. At the next stop, 6 passengers boarded and 2 left; she added 6 to 20 to get 26, then subtracted 2 to get 24. The route map divided the remaining 18 kilometers into 3 equal sections, so she divided 18 by 3 and wrote 6 kilometers per section in her notebook. She added the listed travel times, 12 minutes plus 7 minutes, and recorded 19 minutes. At her stop, Greta closed the notebook, lifted her bag, and stepped onto the pavement.

At seven fifteen, Ibrahim stood beneath the bus shelter while rain drummed on its plastic roof. When the bus arrived, he joined the queue and held his pass against the reader. It flashed red. The driver waved him aside, then admitted the next passenger whose pass produced the same red light. Ibrahim showed the renewal receipt on his phone. The driver glanced at it and pointed toward the pavement. “Off the bus.” Behind Ibrahim, someone sighed. Heat climbed his neck. He had paid yesterday, skipping lunch to cover the fare, and now this man would make him late while letting someone else ride. His fingers closed around the phone until its edges bit his palm. He planted both feet beside the reader and opened the receipt again, enlarging the date with two rigid fingers. The driver reached for the door controls. Ibrahim struck the partition with his flat hand, hard enough to silence the queue. He kept the receipt raised.

Ibrahim reached the bus stop at seven, carrying a brick-red canvas bag beneath a burgundy umbrella. Rain collected along the red metal bench and slid onto the pavement beside his shoes. When the bus arrived, its crimson doors folded inward, revealing maroon flooring and rows of red upholstered seats. He tapped his red travel card against the reader and took a seat beside a window edged with scarlet rubber. Across the aisle, a passenger held a newspaper above a tomato-red shopping basket. Ibrahim placed his bag between his feet and adjusted the cuff of his rust-colored coat. At the next stop, two passengers boarded with red lunch containers tucked under their arms. Sunlight passed through a ruby advertisement on the window, laying a red rectangle across his sleeve. He checked the time on his watch, then stood as the bus approached the red-brick building where he worked.

Ibrahim reached the bus stop at seven and stood beside the timetable. He counted 8 people under the shelter and 5 along the pavement; 8 plus 5 made 13. When 3 boarded an earlier bus, he subtracted 3 from 13 and got 10. His bus arrived with six windows visible along its side. Each window had two sliding panes, so he multiplied 6 by 2 and recorded 12 panes in his notebook. Inside, he took a seat near the middle. The route covered 18 kilometers in 45 minutes; dividing 18 by 45 gave 0.4 kilometers per minute. At the next stop, 7 passengers entered and 4 left, making a net increase of 3. Ibrahim turned a page and counted the remaining stops: 12 before the bridge and 6 after it, totaling 18. He closed the notebook when the bus passed the water tower, then moved his bag beneath his seat.

Ibrahim left his apartment after putting his lunch container into his bag. At the bus stop, he stood beside the timetable and watched a delivery van pull away from the curb. The bus arrived, and he stepped aboard, held his pass against the reader, and walked to a seat near the middle. He placed his bag on his knees. Through the window, he saw shop shutters, bicycles secured to railings, and a worker sweeping a doorway. At the next stop, several passengers boarded while another passenger got off with a folded umbrella. Ibrahim moved his shoes beneath his seat to leave the aisle clear. He adjusted the strap of his bag and looked at the route display above the driver. When the bus reached his stop, he pressed the button, rose from his seat, and exited through the rear doors. He walked along the pavement toward his office building.

At seven each morning, Ibrahim took the number twelve bus along the river road to the printing factory. That Tuesday, he stood beside the rear doors, holding a metal pole while rain striped the windows. As the bus began its descent toward the bridge, the driver pressed the brake pedal twice, then stamped on it. The bus kept gathering speed. Ibrahim watched the driver's shoulders stiffen and his hand pull repeatedly at a lever beside the seat. Ahead, red lights marked a line of stopped traffic. Ibrahim's mouth went dry. He gripped the pole with both hands, but his palms slid against the metal. There was nowhere to step, nothing solid enough to hide behind. He pictured the rear window of the truck ahead bursting into his face. His knees folded as the driver steered toward the empty pavement. When the bus struck the curb, Ibrahim shut his eyes and tucked his head beneath his arms.

Ibrahim reached the coastal bus stop at seven, while seawater moved between the harbor pilings below the pavement. Beyond the shelter, fishing boats crossed the inlet in single file, their hulls leaving narrow bands of foam. He boarded the morning bus, tapped his pass, and took a window seat facing the bay. The route followed the coastline past tidal pools where small crabs moved beneath ribbons of seaweed. At the first stop, two passengers entered carrying canvas bags printed with blue whales. Ibrahim placed his lunch container beside his briefcase as the bus passed a yard stacked with lobster pots. Through the glass, he watched a ferry approach its berth, then checked the time on his watch. The bus continued along the seawall, with low waves folding onto strips of shingle. Near the marine survey office, he pressed the stop button, collected his belongings, and stepped onto the harbor road.

At seven fifteen, Ibrahim stood beneath the bus shelter with a lunch tin and an envelope of application papers. The bus arrived coughing diesel into the October air. He climbed aboard, counted his coins twice, and took a seat beside a window streaked with last night's rain. His phone vibrated just as the bus pulled away. The workshop had written back. He read the first sentence, then pressed his thumb against the screen to keep it still. They had offered him the apprenticeship, with wages enough to leave his second job. A laugh burst out before he could swallow it. He covered his mouth, but another followed. Across the aisle, a passenger glanced up; Ibrahim nodded at her, grinning so broadly his cheeks ached. He folded the application papers into his bag. At the next stop, he paid the fare for someone searching empty pockets, then drummed both heels beneath his seat.

The morning bus carried Ibrahim past shuttered bakeries, roadworks, and rows of rain-darkened houses. He took his usual seat behind the driver and moved his bag off the cushion beside him. For three years, an elderly woman had boarded at the next stop, bringing two peppermints and news of her balcony tomatoes. She had missed the last four mornings. Today the driver passed him a folded notice while they waited at a red light. Her photograph sat above the dates of her life. Ibrahim read the final date twice, then looked toward the stop, where a man stood beneath her usual umbrella of branches. His mouth filled with water he could not swallow. He kept his bag on the floor as passengers crowded aboard. At his office stop, he remained seated, pressing a thumb into the empty cushion's seam. He had never asked her name, and now it was printed in his lap.

The morning bus carried Greta past shuttered bakeries and rows of parked bicycles beneath a low October sky. She sat on the left, as she had every weekday for eleven years, with her lunch bag balanced on her knees. At the next corner, she raised her hand toward the window before remembering there would be nobody to wave back. Her father’s repair shop had been closed since his funeral. This morning, the shop itself was gone. Behind a wire fence lay bricks, splintered shelves, and half the counter where he had taught her to count change. One yellow drawer stood open in the rubble. Greta pressed the stop button, although her office was six stops away. On the pavement, she gripped the fence until its wires marked her palms. She tried to picture his hands opening that drawer. Already, she could remember the brass handle more clearly than his fingers.

On Sunday afternoon, Beatriz played midfield in an amateur football match on the municipal pitch. Her team was one goal down when she intercepted a pass and drove toward the penalty area. A defender hooked her ankle from behind, sending her knees into the gravel beside the grass. The referee waved play on. As she stood, blood running down her shin, he awarded the same defender a free kick for a brush against his shoulder. “Different rules for him?” she asked. The referee showed her a yellow card. Heat climbed her neck. She pressed her tongue against her teeth until her jaw ached. He had watched the tackle; she had seen his eyes follow it. Now her team was losing time while he lectured her about respect. She planted the ball for the restart harder than necessary, then backed away with her fists closed, counting each step because she wanted to march straight back into his path.

Leila’s train crossed the salt plains through the afternoon, twelve hours into a journey that would last until morning. She had paid extra for a sleeper after three weeks of double shifts, and kept the reservation folded inside her ticket. At dusk, a conductor knocked and ordered her into the corridor. A passenger in a tailored coat stood behind him, carrying no bedding. “He needs this compartment,” the conductor said. Leila showed her reservation. He glanced at it, then dropped it onto her suitcase and opened the door wider for the other passenger. Heat climbed her neck. Her jaw tightened until a tooth ached. So her money counted when they took it, but her place counted only until someone better dressed wanted it. She planted her suitcase across the doorway. When the conductor reached for its handle, she slapped her palm over his and held his gaze. Behind her, the neatly made berth remained empty.

At seven fifteen, Ibrahim stood beside the bus shelter as rain streaked the timetable glass. When the bus arrived, he joined the queue with his pass ready. The reader flashed green, but the driver thrust an arm across the aisle. “Pay again.” Ibrahim pointed to the screen and the deduction on his phone. The driver looked past both and waved the next passenger through without checking her ticket. Behind him, someone told him to stop holding everyone up. Heat climbed his neck. He pressed his teeth together until his jaw ached, staring at the green light that had already proved him right. His shift began in twenty minutes; another delay meant another warning. He dropped coins into the machine, each one striking metal harder than necessary. Walking down the aisle, he gripped the receipt so tightly its edge cut his thumb. He pictured laying both charges on the depot counter and refusing to leave.

Lukas sat beside a scratched window as the overnight train crossed the mountains on the thirteenth hour of its journey. Empty cups rattled on his table, and the dark glass reflected rows of sleeping passengers. Then the brakes caught hard enough to throw his bag into the aisle. The train stopped inside a tunnel. For several seconds, nothing moved except a newspaper sliding from someone’s lap. A dull impact sounded overhead. Water began pouring through a seam above the carriage door. Lukas pulled his feet onto the seat as a black stream spread across the floor. He pressed the emergency intercom, but its button stayed dark. Farther down the carriage, someone tugged uselessly at a door handle. His tongue stuck to the roof of his mouth. He pictured the miles of mountain above them, the tunnel filling from both ends. When the lights went out, he gripped the seat until his fingernails bent.

At seven fifteen, Ingrid stood beneath the bus shelter with her work bag and a paper cup of coffee. When the bus arrived, she climbed aboard and held her pass against the reader. It flashed green, but the driver put his hand across the aisle. He demanded another fare. She pointed to the screen; he covered it with his palm and waved the next passenger through without checking anything. Behind her, shoes scraped and someone sighed. Heat climbed Ingrid’s neck. She had renewed that pass yesterday, sacrificing groceries to keep getting to work, and now he treated her like a cheat. Her fingers crushed the cup until coffee spilled over her knuckles. She set it down, planted both feet, and pulled up the receipt on her phone. The driver told her to move. Ingrid held the screen inches from his hand. She would not pay twice to make his morning easier.

At two in the morning, Malik drove a pallet jack between stacked cartons in the warehouse’s north aisle. The overhead lights clicked off behind him, one row at a time. He stopped and checked the timer on his scanner; the building wasn’t scheduled to go dark until six. Somewhere beyond the shelving, a loading door rolled upward. Then came the scrape of metal dragged across concrete. Malik reached for his radio, but a voice crackled through before he pressed the button. “Stay where you are.” He recognized neither the voice nor the channel. At the aisle’s far end, a figure stepped beneath the remaining light, carrying bolt cutters. Another emerged behind him. His tongue stuck to the roof of his mouth. He backed into a carton, sending plastic bottles rattling across the floor. Both figures turned toward the sound. Malik crouched behind the pallet jack, clamping his shaking hand over the scanner’s bright screen, while footsteps approached from both ends.

Andrei entered the museum at ten and took a floor plan from the stand. The first gallery contained 8 cases along one wall and 6 along the other; he added 8 + 6 and recorded 14 cases in his notebook. Each case held 3 pottery fragments, so he multiplied 14 × 3 and obtained 42 fragments. In the next room, a label identified 25 tools, but 7 occupied a separate cabinet. He subtracted 25 − 7 and counted the resulting 18 on the central platform. Upstairs, 36 prints hung in 4 equal rows. He divided 36 ÷ 4 and marked 9 prints per row. He then measured his route on the plan: 5 sections of 12 meters gave 5 × 12 = 60 meters. At the final display, he copied an inventory number, closed the notebook, and returned the floor plan to its stand before leaving through the side entrance.

Dmitri worked the night shift beneath the warehouse’s fluorescent lights, stacking cartons beside loading bay six. At two, the conveyor stopped with a metallic snap. He reached for the wall phone, but a scraping sound came from the locked chemical storeroom. Something struck its door hard enough to shake dust from the frame. Dmitri stepped backward. A thin yellow liquid slid beneath the door and spread toward a loose electrical cable. He knew what the warning labels on those drums meant. His tongue stuck to the roof of his mouth. The nearest exit stood beyond the widening puddle; the other was chained shut for repairs. He pulled the alarm handle. Nothing sounded. Behind the door, another drum toppled, followed by a hiss that grew steadily louder. Dmitri wrapped his sleeve around his hand and struck the window beside him, once, twice, while the cable began to spit blue sparks.

At seven fifteen, Greta stood beneath the bus shelter while rain striped the timetable glass. When the bus arrived, she folded her umbrella and joined the queue, her pass ready between two fingers. The driver waved three people aboard without checking their cards, then blocked her with his arm. Her pass had a faded corner; he demanded cash. She showed him the valid date, holding it beneath his dashboard light. He turned away and tapped the fare box. Behind her, shoes shuffled. Heat climbed her neck until her collar seemed too tight. She counted coins onto the tray, each one striking harder than the last. He had seen the date. He had simply decided she would pay twice. As the bus lurched forward, she gripped the rail so fiercely her knuckles blanched. She photographed his badge number and opened the complaint form, refusing to let her shaking thumb mistype a single digit.

Kenji stood beneath the museum’s glass dome beside a row of bronze statues. He had saved for weeks to see the upstairs exhibition, and his ticket included admission. At the staircase, an attendant stopped him and pointed to his scuffed work boots. “Not in those,” she said. Behind him, visitors in muddy hiking shoes passed without a glance. Kenji held out his ticket, then the printed policy permitting ordinary footwear. She folded the paper against his palm and waved him toward the exit. Heat climbed his neck. His fingers tightened until the ticket tore along its crease. So their dirt belonged here, but his did not. He planted both boots on the marble and asked for a supervisor, each word clipped hard between his teeth. When the attendant reached for his elbow, he pulled away. He would not let her steer him outside as though he had slipped in without paying.

Bruno played midfield on a municipal pitch where crooked nets hung between rusted posts and substitutes sat on kit bags. With five minutes left, he intercepted a pass and drove toward the penalty area. A defender hooked both arms around his waist and dragged him down. The referee waved play on. Bruno sprang up, grass stuck to his cheek, and pointed at the torn seam of his shirt. “You were looking straight at him.” The referee showed him a yellow card while the defender covered a grin with his hand. Heat climbed Bruno’s neck. His jaw locked so tightly that his back teeth ached. Apparently, getting hauled down counted for nothing; objecting was the offense. He crushed a fistful of his shirt, then released it before the fabric split further. When play restarted, he sprinted after the ball, each breath scraping his throat, unable to stop replaying that hidden grin.

Priya played left wing in an amateur football match on a school field bordered by parked bicycles. With five minutes remaining, she slipped past a defender and drove the ball inside the post. The referee blew his whistle and pointed upfield. Offside. She had started behind the ball; everyone along the touchline had seen it. The defender covered his mouth, laughing, then slapped the referee’s shoulder as he passed. They wore identical club jackets beside the bench. Heat climbed Priya’s neck. Her jaw locked so tightly that her back teeth ached. “Ask your linesman,” she said. The referee waved her away without looking. So that was how their Saturday worked: his friend made a mistake, and she paid for it. She planted herself in his path, fists pressed against her thighs. When he reached for a card, she stepped aside and sprinted after the ball, each footfall punching mud from the turf.

Ana’s train crossed the mountain plateau on the second night of its journey, its windows silvered by sleet. She had spent the day counting tunnels and folding the corners of a timetable. Near midnight, a sharp crack rang beneath her carriage. Her cup slid off the table. Then the train gathered speed, although the timetable showed a station just beyond the descending curve. Outside, sparks streamed against the glass. A conductor hurried down the aisle, pulling at a radio that answered only with static. Ana gripped his sleeve; he barely stopped. “Get down between the seats.” She crouched, her knees striking the floor, and tried to swallow through a throat that had closed tight. The wheels shrieked. Ahead, through the connecting doorway, carriage lights swung violently from side to side. She pictured the ravine they had crossed that afternoon and pressed both hands over her head, waiting for the floor to vanish.

At seven fifteen, Viktor stood near the rear doors of the morning bus as it crossed the hill above the railway station. His lunch bag swung from one wrist, and he checked his watch between stops. Then the driver pressed the brake pedal twice, bent forward, and pressed it again. The bus kept gathering speed. Ahead, red lights marked the intersection at the bottom of the hill. Viktor watched the driver pull a lever with both hands. Nothing changed. His mouth dried so quickly that his tongue caught against his teeth. He gripped a pole, but his fingers slipped on the polished steel. A delivery truck began turning across their lane. There would not be room. He pictured the windows bursting inward and pulled his lunch bag against his chest, absurdly, as though it could shield him. The horn sounded continuously. Viktor crouched behind a seat and could no longer make himself look.

Malik began his night shift at the warehouse by counting cartons beneath the loading bay lights. One pallet held 24 cartons and another held 18; he added 24 + 18 = 42 and entered the total on his sheet. From a stack of 70 empty trays, he removed 16, calculating 70 − 16 = 54 before moving the remainder beside a conveyor. Each of 8 shelves required 6 dividers, so he wrote 8 × 6 = 48 and collected that quantity from storage. Next, he distributed 96 labels among 12 bins, using 96 ÷ 12 = 8 labels per bin. At midnight, he measured an aisle in three sections: 9 + 11 + 10 = 30 meters. He recorded the measurement, returned the tape to its hook, and swept along the marked walking route. The ventilation fans continued turning while he arranged the next set of cartons for counting.

Ibrahim boarded the morning bus at 7:20 and sat beside a window. The route had 18 stops, and he subtracted the 5 already passed from 18, leaving 13 before the terminal. He counted 8 passengers near the front and 11 farther back; 8 plus 11 made 19. At the next stop, 3 passengers stepped down, so 19 minus 3 left 16. Along the avenue, he counted 6 rows of trees with 4 trees in each row and calculated that 6 times 4 equaled 24. The bus covered a marked stretch of 900 meters in 3 minutes; 900 divided by 3 gave 300 meters per minute. He recorded each calculation in a small notebook resting on his knee. Between two intersections, he added 12 parked bicycles to 7 outside a bakery and wrote 19 beneath the other figures. When the bus reached his stop, Ibrahim closed the notebook and stepped onto the pavement.

Kenji entered the museum at ten and took a floor plan from the counter. The first gallery contained 8 cases along one wall and 7 along another; he calculated 8 + 7 = 15 cases and marked the total beside the diagram. In the pottery section, 24 vessels occupied 6 shelves, so he worked out 24 ÷ 6 = 4 vessels per shelf. He counted 18 labels beneath a group of fragments, then subtracted the 5 labels that referred to missing pieces: 18 − 5 = 13. Upstairs, each of 9 panels displayed 3 photographs. He wrote 9 × 3 = 27 in his notebook. A bench stood between two doorways. Kenji sat there and checked the route: 12 rooms on the plan minus 8 already visited left 4 rooms. He passed through those rooms in numerical order, returned the floor plan, and left through the museum’s side entrance.

Carlos had spent sixteen hours aboard the overnight train as it crossed the mountains toward the coast. By midnight, the dining carriage had closed, and most passengers slept beneath folded coats. He was watching rain streak the glass when a metallic crack sounded under his seat. The carriage lurched, throwing a cup into the aisle. Then the steady clatter became a grinding shriek, and the train gathered speed downhill. Carlos gripped the table until his fingers ached. Outside, sparks streamed past the windows. A conductor stumbled through the door, pulled an emergency handle, and pulled it again. Nothing changed. Carlos remembered the narrow bridge marked on the route map, somewhere below them in the gorge. His mouth dried so completely that he could not swallow. He shoved his bag beneath the seat, crouched behind the table, and braced his shoulders against it. Through the glass, two rows of bridge lights rushed closer.

At two in the morning, Fatima scanned cartons beneath the warehouse strip lights while rain tapped the loading bays. She had almost finished her aisle when a forklift struck the far end of the shelving. The driver backed away, leaving a bent upright and a thin stream of powdered concrete. Above her, six pallets of bagged cement shifted together. Fatima lowered her scanner. A bolt pinged against the floor beside her shoe, and the aisle gate, twisted by the impact, would not open. She pulled until the wire mesh cut her palms. The shelving gave a long metallic groan. Her tongue stuck to the roof of her mouth; each breath stopped halfway into her chest. There was nowhere beneath those pallets that her body could fit and survive. She dropped flat and crawled toward the narrow gap under the gate, dragging one boot behind her as another bolt fell.

Mira stood beneath the museum’s glass dome beside a display of bronze ships. She had just leaned closer to read a label when a sharp crack snapped overhead. A white line spread across one pane, then branched into three. Somewhere behind the walls, metal groaned. The attendant dropped his booklet and waved everyone toward the corridor, but a security shutter crashed down across its entrance. Mira stopped so abruptly that her shoes slid on the marble. Above her, another pane split. She pictured those enormous sheets falling edge first, cutting through coats and raised hands. Her tongue stuck to the roof of her mouth. She pulled at a locked side door until the handle bruised her palm, then spotted a stone arch beyond the display. Keeping her eyes down, she crawled beneath it and covered her head. The first glittering fragments struck the floor where she had been standing.

At two in the morning, Fatima stacked cartons beneath the warehouse’s fluorescent lights while rain tapped the loading doors. She had spent six hours clearing another worker’s backlog, skipping her break to finish before the trucks arrived. When the supervisor checked his clipboard, he crossed out her overtime.

“Your scanner shows too many pauses.”

Fatima pointed to the broken conveyor, the handwritten tally, the pallets she had dragged alone. He shrugged and handed her another picking list. Behind him, a worker who had slept through an hour received approval for extra pay.

Heat climbed Fatima’s neck. Her fingers tightened around the list until the paper split beneath her thumb. So her work counted when boxes needed moving, but vanished when wages came due. She set the scanner down hard enough to rattle its cradle, photographed the tally and the crossed-out hours, then planted herself beside the supervisor’s desk. The next pallet could wait.
